review_text_clean: Chittagong's historic 'Elephant Bungalow' Everyone wants to see such a natural scene with high mountains all around, lush greenery and the sound of birds chirping. If you move forward a little, you might think that a huge elephant is standing with its trunk raised. Although it looks alive from a distance, when you get a little closer, you will see a 131-year-old duplex house built in the shape of an elephant. Although it looks exactly like an elephant, it is actually an ancient building built of bricks and stones. It is also known as the 'Elephant Bungalow' to the locals. This beautiful house, located on the hills of CRB, the lungs of Chittagong, has an ancient history. This century-old history may not be known to many. Looking into history, it is known that in 1893, the construction of the railway from Chittagong to Feni began under the British engineer Brownzer. Engineer Brownzer himself built the bungalow for the residence of railway officials in the mid-19th century. However, due to the passage of time, the bungalow has become uninhabitable today. If you walk forward through the Ladies Club in the Lalkhan Bazar area of ​​Chittagong and go a little to the right, you will see this elephant bungalow. Currently, this elephant bungalow, which is part of the history and heritage of Chittagong, is in a dilapidated state. There is no maintenance, as a result, the beauty of the bungalow is being lost. It has been seen on site that the bungalow has a total of 12 round windows in the front and back. In addition, there are two round holes on both sides of the balcony built in the shape of an elephant's trunk, which look a lot like the eyes of an elephant. This duplex building has 4 bedrooms on the ground floor and one on the second floor. Currently, all the doors and windows of the establishment are broken and rusty. All the windows made of wood are in a dilapidated state. In addition, moss has grown all over the walls of the building, and the plaster has started to fall off. Various types of dirt and dry leaves are piled up all around the house. A railway employee now lives in a bedroom inside this aesthetic bungalow. Many visitors come to see the elephant bungalow in the afternoon. In addition to taking pictures, various short films are often shot here. Built with 'ferro' cement in the mid-19th century, this bungalow is still in a very strong condition even though it is 132 years old. However, the beauty of this tradition is being lost day by day due to lack of maintenance. This structure is also painted gray to match the color of the elephant's body, but due to lack of maintenance, the color of the building has now faded. This elephant bungalow has been lying around for years, without any steps or proper maintenance. If initiatives are taken to preserve this aesthetic architecture, it will become more attractive to visitors. Author: Student, Department of Journalism and Media Studies, Port City International University, Chittagong.
review_text_original: চট্টগ্রামের ঐতিহাসিক ‘হাতির বাংলো’ চারপাশে উঁচু পাহাড়, সবুজের সমারোহ ও পাখির কিচিরমিচির শব্দ, এমন প্রাকৃতিক দৃশ্য দেখার ইচ্ছে সবার মধ্যেই আছে। এর মধ্যে দিয়ে একটু সামনে এগিয়ে গেলেই দূর থেকে দেখে যে কারো মনে হতে পারে বিশাল একটি হাতি শুঁড় তুলে দাঁড়িয়ে আছে। দূর থেকে জীবিত মনে হলেও, সামান্য কাছে যেতেই দেখা মিলবে হাতির আদলে নির্মিত ১৩১ বছরের পুরোনো একটি ডুপ্লেক্স বাড়ি। দেখতে অবিকল হাতির মতো মনে হলেও এটি মূলত ইট-পাথরে নির্মিত একটি প্রাচীন ভবন। স্থানীয়দের কাছে এটি ‘হাতির বাংলো’ নামেও পরিচিত। চট্টগ্রামের ফুসফুসখ্যাত সিআরবির পাহাড়ে দৃষ্টিনন্দন আদি এই বাড়ির সঙ্গে জড়িয়ে আছে প্রাচীন ইতিহাস। শতবর্ষ পুরোনো এই ইতিহাস হয়তো অনেকেরই অজানা। ইতিহাস ঘেটে জানা গেছে, ১৮৯৩ সালে চট্টগ্রাম থেকে ফেনী পর্যন্ত রেলপথ নির্মাণ কাজ শুরু হয় বৃটিশ প্রকৌশলী ব্রাউনজারের অধীনে। ঊনিশ শতকের মাঝামাঝিতে রেলওয়ে কর্মকর্তাদের বসবাসের জন্যই বাংলোটি নিজেই নির্মাণ করেন প্রকৌশলী ব্রাউনজার। তবে কালের আবহমানে বাংলোটি আজ বসবাসের অযোগ্য হয়ে পড়েছে। চট্টগ্রামের লালখান বাজার এলাকার লেডিস ক্লাবের ভেতর দিয়ে সামনে এগিয়ে হাতের ডানে সামান্য গেলেই চোখে পড়বে এই হাতির বাংলো। বর্তমানে চট্টগ্রামের ইতিহাস ও ঐতিহ্যের অংশ এই হাতির বাংলো পড়ে আছে অনেকটা জীর্ণশীর্ণ অবস্থায়। নেই কোনো রক্ষণাবেক্ষণ, ফলে হারাতে বসেছে বাংলোটির সৌন্দর্য। সরেজমিনে দেখা গেছে,বাংলোটির সামনে ও পেছনের অংশ মিলিয়ে মোট ১২টি গোলআকৃতির জানালা আছে। এছাড়া হাতির শুঁড়ের আদলে নির্মিত বারান্দার দু’পাশেও আছে গোলাকার দুটো ছিদ্র, যা দেখতে অনেকটাই হাতির চোখের মতো। ডুপ্লেক্স এই ভবনের নীচতলায় ৪টি ও দোতলায় একটি শয়নকক্ষ আছে। বর্তমানে স্থাপনাটির সবক’টি দরজা-জানালাই ভেঙে পড়ার পাশাপাশি মরিচা ধরেছে। কাঠ দিয়ে নির্মিত সব জানালাগুলোই পড়ে আছে জরাজীর্ণ অবস্থায়। এছাড়া ভবনের দেয়ালজুড়ে পড়েছে শ্যাওলা, খসে পড়তে শুরু করেছে পলেস্তারা। বাড়ির চারপাশজুড়ে জমে আছে বিভিন্ন ময়লা আর শুকনো পাতা। নান্দনিক এই বাংলোতে এখন একজন রেলওয়ে কর্মচারী ভেতরের একটি শয়নকক্ষে কোনো রকমে থাকেন। বিকেল হলেই অনেক দর্শনার্থী হাতির বাংলো দেখতে ছুটে আসেন। দর্শনার্থীরা ছবি তোলার পাশাপাশি এখানে অনেক সময় বিভিন্ন শর্টফিল্মের শুটিংও হয়ে থাকে। ঊনিশ শতকের মাঝামাঝিতে ‘ফেরো’ সিমেন্ট দিয়ে নির্মিত এই বাংলোর ১৩২ বছর পেরিয়ে গেলেও এখনো বেশ মজবুত অবস্থায় আছে। তবে রক্ষণাবেক্ষণের অভাবে দিনদিন হারাতে বসেছে এই ঐতিহ্যের সৌন্দর্য। হাতির গায়ের রঙের সঙ্গে মিলিয়ে এই স্থাপনাতেও ধূসর রং করা হয়, তবে রক্ষণাবেক্ষণের অভাবে ভবনের রং পুরোটাই এখন বিবর্ণ ধারণ করেছে। বছরের পর বছর ধরে পড়ে আছে এই হাতির বাংলো, নেই কোনো পদক্ষেপ কিংবা যথাযথ রক্ষণাবেক্ষণ। নান্দনিক এই স্থাপত্য সংরক্ষণের উদ্যোগ নিলে এটি review_text_clean: Chinamati Hills, located in the Bijoypur area of ​​​​Susang Durgapur in Netrakona district, are famous for their unique natural beauty. It is mainly a mineral area, where white clay hills and mountains can be seen. Since 1957, commercial extraction of chinamati has started here, which is used as the main raw material in the ceramic industry. Due to soil excavation, many small and large lakes have been created in different places on the hill. Due to the white soil, the water of the lakes is sometimes clear blue, and sometimes greenish blue or pink, which presents an extraordinary scene. Its length is about 15.5 kilometers and width is 600 meters. The Someshwari River is next to this hill, which enhances its beauty many times over. Currently, it is known as a popular tourist destination, where numerous tourists come every day to enjoy the charming view of white clay hills and colorful water lakes.
review_text_original: নেত্রকোণা জেলার সুসং দুর্গাপুরের বিজয়পুর এলাকায় অবস্থিত চিনামাটির পাহাড় তার অনন্য প্রাকৃতিক সৌন্দর্যের জন্য বিখ্যাত। এটি মূলত একটি খনিজ অঞ্চল, যেখানে সাদা রঙের চিনামাটির টিলা ও পাহাড় দেখতে পাওয়া যায়। ১৯৫৭ সাল থেকে এখানে বাণিজ্যিক ভিত্তিতে চিনামাটি উত্তোলন শুরু হয়, যা সিরামিক শিল্পের প্রধান কাঁচামাল হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হয়। মাটি খননের ফলে এই পাহাড়ের বুকে বিভিন্ন স্থানে ছোট-বড় অনেক হ্রদের সৃষ্টি হয়েছে। সাদা মাটির কারণে হ্রদগুলোর পানি কোথাও স্বচ্ছ নীল, আবার কোথাও সবুজাভ নীল বা গোলাপি রঙের দেখায়, যা এক অসাধারণ দৃশ্যের অবতারণা করে। এর দৈর্ঘ্য প্রায় ১৫.৫ কিলোমিটার এবং প্রস্থ ৬০০ মিটার। এই পাহাড়ের পাশেই রয়েছে সোমেশ্বরী নদী, যা এর সৌন্দর্যকে আরও বহুগুণ বাড়িয়ে তোলে। বর্তমানে এটি একটি জনপ্রিয় পর্যটন কেন্দ্র হিসেবে পরিচিত, যেখানে প্রতিদিন অসংখ্য পর্যটক সাদা মাটির পাহাড় এবং রঙিন জলের হ্রদের মনোমুগ্ধকর দৃশ্য উপভোগ করতে আসে।

It is about 15.5 km long and 600 m wide [1, 14]. Mining and use: Kohinoor Aluminium Works was the first to commercially mine this soil in 1960 [1]. Later, BCIC took over mining in 1973 [1]. Located on the banks of the Buriganga River, it was the official residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka, with construction beginning in 1859 and completing in 1872. Significance: Ahsan Manzil is a significant cultural heritage site in Bangladesh, offering insight into the country's colonial history. Its restoration in the late 1980s, aided by old photographs, saved it from disrepair and allowed for its preservation as a museum for future generations.

review_text_clean: Ahsan Manzil, known as the Pink Palace, is one of Dhaka’s most famous landmarks. It sits on the bank of the Buriganga River in Kumartoli and was once the official residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka. Built between 1859 and 1872 in a blend of Mughal and European styles, it now serves as a branch museum under the Bangladesh National Museum. The palace’s history mirrors the rise and fall of Dhaka’s aristocracy. The site first belonged to a Mughal landlord named Sheikh Enayetullah, and later to French traders in the 18th century. In 1830, Khwaja Alimullah bought it, and his son Khwaja Abdul Ghani turned it into the grand palace we see today, naming it after his own son, Ahsanullah. The building was badly damaged by a tornado in 1888 but was rebuilt with its now-iconic dome. Over time, it became a political center where major decisions and meetings were held, including early gatherings of the All India Muslim League. After the Nawabs’ decline, the palace fell into neglect until it was restored and opened as a museum in 1992. The palace has two main parts — Rangmahal, which contained formal rooms like the drawing and guest rooms, and Andarmahal, which housed private areas like the dining and music rooms. A wooden bridge once connected the two. The large central dome, shaped like a lotus bud, rises above the structure and is one of Dhaka’s most recognizable sights. Visitors can tour the museum for a small fee (ranging from 40৳ for locals to 500৳ for foreign tourists). It’s open Saturday to Wednesday and on Fridays in the afternoon, but closed on Thursdays. A one-hour visit is enough to explore its galleries and enjoy the palace’s beauty. Its location in Old Dhaka also makes it easy to visit along with nearby attractions like Lalbagh Fort and the Star Mosque.

Before today I had visited it so many times. It is the former residence and seat of the Nawab of Dhaka. In the Mughal Empire, Sheikh Enayet ullah, Zamindar of the Jamalpur, Porgona district had a garden house on this property and added a palace which he called Rangmahal. After his death his son Sheikh Moti ullah was sold to French Traders. They erected a trading house beside the property. In the year of 1835 Nawba Abdul Ghani's father Khwaja Alimullah purchased the property from the French traders. He had renovated it and started living there as a “Nawab” house. In the year of 1872 Nawab Khwaja Abdul Ghani also renovated it and named the property as “Ahsan Manzil” for his son Khwaja Ahsan Ullah. He also continued renovations; the old building was renamed Ondor Mohol and the new building was called Rangmahal. The Government of Bangladesh acquired the palace and property in 1985 and also renovated it. Renovations were completed in the year of 1992 and ownership was transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum. Now it is an old Dhaka heritage site of Bangladesh. It is always busy with national visitors and foreign tourists. It is open at 10:30 am and closed at 0530pm regularly. Thursday is a weekly holiday. Entrance fee adult Tk40/, Child Tk20/ for hoste, SARAC Tk300/ and foreign Tk 500/ each only. However, the palace was reconstructed and restored under the supervision of Lord Curzon, the then Viceroy of India. The reconstruction was completed in 1901, and the palace regained its former glory. In 1985, the Bangladesh government converted Ahsan Manzil into a museum to showcase the rich heritage and history of Dhaka and its Nawabi era. The architectural style of Ahsan Manzil is a fusion of Mughal and European influences, predominantly reflecting the Indo-Saracenic architectural style. The palace complex covers an area of around 5 acres and features a magnificent pink-colored building with a distinct dome and grand portico. Unfortunately, Ahsan Manzil suffered extensive damage during a tornado in 1888 and a devastating earthquake in 1897. However, the palace was reconstructed and restored under the supervision of Lord Curzon, the then Viceroy of India. The reconstruction was completed in 1901, and the palace regained its former glory. In 1985, the Bangladesh government converted Ahsan Manzil into a museum to showcase the rich heritage and history of Dhaka and its Nawabi era. The museum exhibits a wide range of artifacts, photographs, paintings, furniture, and other items that provide insights into the lifestyle, culture, and traditions of the Nawab family and the bygone era. Ahsan Manzil is a popular tourist attraction, drawing visitors who are interested in exploring the architectural beauty, historical significance, and cultural heritage of Bangladesh. The museum offers a glimpse into the opulent lifestyle of the Nawabs and provides a fascinating journey back in time. review_text_clean: Shashi Lodge is one of the most important historical structures in Mymensingh. Based on verified information, we have prepared a 200+ word Google Maps review. Shashi Lodge is a famous historical palace and architectural monument in Mymensingh city, also known locally as Mymensingh Rajbari. Maharaja Suryakanta Acharya Chowdhury, a descendant of the Muktagachha zamindar family, built this palace in the name of his adopted son Shashikanta Acharya. The original two-story building, built in the late 19th century, was severely damaged in the terrible earthquake of 1897. Later, Shashikanta Acharya built a new building on the same site, the construction of which was completed around 1905 and its beautification and renovation were carried out in 1911. Spread over an area of ​​about 9 acres, the architecture of Shashi Lodge shows the traces of European influence as well as the opulence of the zamindari period. The magnificent arches of the entrance, spacious green courtyard, ornate fountains, old ponds, marble construction, large halls, elaborate doors and windows, and historical interior architecture attract visitors. Various works of art and historical monuments associated with the palace have also increased its importance. Shashi Lodge was declared a protected monument of the Department of Archaeology in 1989. Later, the activities of the Mymensingh Museum were also added to it. As a result, it is not just an old landlord's house, but an important monument of the history, zamindari culture, architecture, and archaeological heritage of Mymensingh. As a historical monument, the preservation, cleanliness, and security of the Shashi Lodge are very important. For history and architecture lovers, Shashi Lodge is a must-see place on a trip to Mymensingh. Combining the palace's historical atmosphere, architectural style, and long past, one can experience an important chapter in the history of the zamindari of Mymensingh by coming here. 🏛️🌿📜

review_text_clean: Bijoypur White Clay Hill. This is a unique and beautiful place in Birishiri and is constantly playing a role in the national economy. The White Clay Hill is one of the most spectacular places in Birishiri. Here is the China Clay Hill, whose chest has been torn open by this blue-green water lake. The color in the middle of the white clay has made it even darker. However, you will not be able to see this beautiful scene just by coming to Birishiri. You will have to go a little further to Bijoypur China Clay Hill. There are China Clay mines in Bijoypur and its surrounding areas of Durgapur Upazila. China Clay is basically the raw material of the ceramic industry. According to the 1957 information of the Mineral Resources Bureau, the reserves of China Clay in this area are about 2.4 million 40 thousand metric tons. It was said at that time that it is possible to meet the three hundred years' demand of Bangladesh with this. A few private companies are extracting China Clay here with permission from the Mineral Resources Development Bureau. Thousands of workers are working on mining projects every day. Then it is transported to the ceramic industry factories. These hills or mountains of china clay are very attractive to see. The color of the clay in Bahari. Red, white, blue. It is like another natural environment. The white clay of Bijoypur is located in Aarapara and Maijpara mouzas of Kullagara Union, 7 kilometers northwest of Durgapur Upazila Parishad. This is one of the largest mineral areas of white clay as a natural resource in Bangladesh. This mineral area is about 15.5 kilometers long and 600 meters wide across small hills and plains. According to the information of the Mineral Resources Development Bureau, the amount of white clay in this area in 1957 was estimated at 24 lakh 70 thousand metric tons, which can meet the needs of Bangladesh for 300 years. You can reach the plain clay area of ​​Bijoypur by crossing the Someshwari River and taking a rickshaw or Honda through a semi-unpaved road.
review_text_original: বিজয়পুর সাদা মাটির পাহাড়। এটি বিরিশিরির অনন্য সুন্দর একটি স্থান সেই সাথে জাতীয় অর্থনীতিতে ভূমিকা রাখছে প্রতিনিয়ত। সাদামাটির পাহাড় বিরিশিরির অন্যতম দর্শনীয় স্থানগুলোর মধ্যে অন্যতম। এখানে চীনামাটির পাহাড়, যার বুক চিরে জেগে উঠেছে এই নীলচে-সবুজ পানির হ্রদ। সাদা মাটির মাঝে রঙটাকে যেন আরও বেশি গাঢ় করে দিয়েছে। তবে বিরিশিরি এসেই আপনি এ সুন্দর দৃশ্য আপনি দেখতে পারবেন না। আপনাকে যেতে হবে আরেকটু দূর বিজয়পুর চীনা মাটির পাহাড়ে। দুর্গাপুর উপজেলার বিজয়পুর ও এর আশপাশের এলাকায় রয়েছে চিনামাটির খনি। চিনামাটি মূলতঃ সিরামিক শিল্পের কাঁচামাল। খনিজ সম্পদ ব্যুরোর ১৯৫৭ সালের তথ্যানুযায়ী, এ এলাকায় চিনামাটির মজুদ প্রায় ২৪ লাখ ৪০ হাজার মেট্রিক টন। এটি দিয়ে বাংলাদেশের তিনশ বছরের চাহিদা পূরণ সম্ভব বলে তখন বলা হয়েছিল। খনিজ সম্পদ উন্নয়ন ব্যুরো থেকে অনুমতি নিয়ে কয়েকটি বেসরকারি কোম্পানী এখানকার চিনামাটি আহরণ করছে। প্রতিদিন হাজার হাজার শ্রমিক মাটি খননের কাজ করছে খনিজ প্রকল্পগুলোতে। এরপর তা পরিবহন করে নিয়ে যাওয়া হচ্ছে সিরামিক শিল্পের কারখানাগুলোতে। চিনামাটির এসব টিলা বা পাহাড় দেখতে খুবই মনোমুগ্ধকর। বাহারি এর মাটির রঙ। লাল, সাদা, নীলাভ। এ যেন প্রকৃতিক আরেক নিসর্গ। দূর্গাপুর উপজেলা পরিষদ থেকে ৭ কিলোমিটার উত্তর-পশ্চিমে কুল্লাগড়া ইউনিয়নের আড়াপাড়া ও মাইজপাড়া মৌজায় বিজয়পুরের সাদা মাটি অবস্থিত। বাংলাদেশের মধ্যে প্রকৃতির সম্পদ হিসেবে সাদা মাটির অন্যতম বৃহৎখনিজ অঞ্চল এটি। ছোট বড় টিলা-পাহাড় ও সমতল ভূমি জুড়ে প্রায় ১৫.৫ কিলোমিটার দীর্ঘ ও ৬০০ মিটার প্রস্থ এই খনিজ অঞ্চল। খনিজ সম্পদ উন্নয়ন ব্যুরোর তথ্য অনুযায়ী ১৯৫৭ সালে এই অঞ্চলে সাদামাটির পরিমাণ ধরা হয় ২৪ লক্ষ ৭০ হাজার মেট্রিক টন, যা বাংলাদেশের ৩ শত বৎসরের চাহিদা পুরণ করতে পারে। সোমেশ্বরী নদী পার হয়ে রিক্সা বা হোন্ডায় অর্ধ কাচা-পাকা রাস্তা দিয়ে বিজয়পুরের সাদামাটি অঞ্চলে যাওয়া যায়।

review_text_clean: Brief Description: Bijoypur white clay is located in Arapara and Maijpara mouzas of Kullagara Union, 7 kilometers northwest of Durgapur Upazila Parishad. This is one of the largest mineral areas of white clay as a natural resource in Bangladesh. This mineral area is about 15.5 kilometers long and 600 meters wide across small and large hills and plains. According to the Mineral Resources Development Bureau, the amount of white clay in this area in 1957 was estimated to be 24.7 million metric tons, which can meet the needs of Bangladesh for 300 years. Background and History: Although the ancient history of Chinese clay is not known, the work of extracting this soil started in 1957. In 1960, an organization named Kohinoor Aluminum Works was the first to start extracting this soil. Later, BCIC joined in extracting this soil in 1973. Currently, 9 companies are working to extract this soil. About 300 workers are involved in extracting this soil. The beautiful beauty of different colored soil, water and nature captivates the mind. White, pink, yellow, purple, brown, and blue colored hills of soil delight the eyes. Tribal settlements are spread throughout the plain area. How to get there: From Dhaka, take a bus to Mymensingh, Mymensingh via Shyamganj to Durgapur or from Dhaka, take a bus to Netrokona, from Netrokona to Durgapur. Then, cross the Someshwari River and take a rickshaw or motorbike to reach the plain area of ​​Bijoypur via a semi-unpaved road.

review_text_clean: Naval Sea Beach (Chittagong) is a fantastic coastal spot, and the transition from evening to night here offers two completely different, amazing vibes. The Evening Vibe: It starts off incredibly lively and scenic. It’s the perfect time to sit on the concrete blocks, enjoy the cool sea breeze, and watch a beautiful sunset over the water. The Night Vibe: As darkness falls, the atmosphere shifts into a much more relaxed, peaceful, and cooler hangout spot. Sitting by the shore under the night sky with the sound of the waves is deeply therapeutic. The Ultimate Food Highlights: You absolutely cannot visit this beach without diving into its famous street food culture. The local stalls serve up some of the best seaside snacks: Crab Fry & Fish Fry: Freshly caught, heavily spiced, and fried crisp right in front of you. It is a seafood lover's paradise. Peyaju: Piping hot, extra crunchy, and perfectly spiced—making it the ultimate accompaniment to a warm cup of tea by the sea. Verdict: Whether you want to enjoy a buzzing evening sunset or a quiet night-time sea breeze, Naval Beach is highly recommended for its great food and unmatched coastal energy!

review_text_clean: Panam Nagar – The Lost City of Bengal / El Dorado of Bengal. Panam Nagar, located in Sonargaon, Narayanganj, is one of the most fascinating heritage sites in Bangladesh. Often called the “Lost City,” it offers a rare glimpse into the golden days of Bengal’s trading history. This ancient township was built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by wealthy Hindu merchants who thrived during the colonial period. They constructed elegant residential mansions, showcasing a remarkable mix of Mughal, British colonial, and traditional Bengali architecture. The main street of Panam Nagar stretches about 600 meters and is lined with 52 historic buildings, each carrying the scars of time yet still reflecting their former grandeur. Many houses feature ornamental facades, large wooden doors, arched windows, carved pillars, and intricate brickwork. Walking through the deserted street almost feels like traveling back in time, where one can imagine horse-drawn carriages and busy merchants once filling the area. Historically, Sonargaon itself was the capital of Bengal during the medieval Sultanate era and a vital hub of the world-famous Muslin trade. Merchants from across Asia and Europe came here to trade textiles, spices, and other goods. Panam Nagar represents a later chapter of that heritage, where affluent traders settled and displayed their prosperity through architecture. However, following political changes, communal riots, and the Partition of 1947, Panam Nagar was abandoned and fell into decline. Today, it stands as a silent witness to centuries of history, prosperity, and eventual decline. What makes Panam Nagar special is not only the architectural beauty but also the atmosphere. The abandoned mansions, overgrown with trees and plants, create an almost cinematic experience—haunting yet beautiful. For visitors, photographers, and history enthusiasts, it is one of the most photogenic and culturally rich places in Bangladesh. 📍 How to Get There from Dhaka: Panam Nagar is only about 27 km southeast of Dhaka, making it a perfect half-day or day trip. From Gulistan bus terminal, you can take a local bus ( Doyel / Sodesh / Borak) heading to Mograpara, Sonargaon (1–1.5 hours depending on traffic). From Sonargaon, you can take a rickshaw directly to Panam Nagar’s entrance costing about 20/30 Tk per head. 🎟 Ticket Price: Locals: 20 BDT SAARC Nationals: 100 BDT Foreigners: 300 BDT ⏰ Visiting Hours: Open from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (closed on Wednesdays, and half-day on Thursdays). 🌿 Nearby Attractions: Sonargaon Folk Art & Craft Museum: Showcasing Bangladesh’s traditional crafts and heritage. Goaldi Mosque: A beautiful 15th-century mosque with unique terracotta work. Meghna River boat rides: A relaxing way to end your Sonargaon trip. ✨ Overall Experience: Panam Nagar is not just a tourist spot, but a journey through time. It tells the story of Bengal’s trade, culture, and the rise and fall of a community. While many buildings are in ruins, the government and archaeological department have started preservation efforts, making it a more organized and educational site for visitors. If you are in Dhaka, Panam Nagar is one of the must-visit heritage destinations to truly understand the history and culture of Bengal. Highly recommended for short tour.

review_text_clean: Panam City: A Historic Heritage of Bengal Panam City, located in the historic town of Sonargaon in Narayanganj, Bangladesh. It's one of the most remarkable heritage sites of the region. This ancient trading settlement reflects centuries of Bengal’s political, cultural and architectural history. The historical roots of this region go back to the 13th century, when Sonargaon became an important capital and commercial center during the era of the Bengal Sultanate. The area later came under the influence of the famous Baro-Bhuiyan confederacy led by Isa Khan in the 16th century, who resisted the expansion of the Mughal Empire. The buildings that stand in Panam City today were mostly constructed in the 19th century during the period of the British Raj. Wealthy Hindu merchants built elegant residential and commercial houses here, making the area a thriving center of textile trade, particularly famous for the legendary muslin of Bengal. Along a single narrow street, about 52 historic buildings were built, featuring a unique blend of Mughal, European, and colonial architectural styles. Over time, economic and political changes caused the city to be gradually abandoned during the mid-20th century, leaving behind a silent yet fascinating historical landscape. Today Panam City is preserved by the Department of Archaeology of Bangladesh and recognized as one of the country’s most valuable heritage sites. Walking through Panam City feels like stepping back in time. The old brick mansions, decorative facades, and quiet atmosphere beautifully narrate the story of Bengal’s rich past.

review_text_clean: Nestled in the heart of Sonargaon, Narayanganj, just 30 kilometers from Dhaka, lies a hauntingly beautiful ghost town that whispers stories of grandeur, culture, and decline — Panam City (also known as Panam Nagar). Once a vibrant center of trade and aristocratic life during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, this historic city now stands as a striking example of Bangladesh’s colonial architectural heritage. A Glimpse into History Panam City was developed in the late 1800s during the British colonial era. It was primarily inhabited by wealthy Hindu merchants, zamindars, and landowners who built elegant mansions and commercial buildings in European-inspired styles. This area formed part of the ancient city of Sonargaon, which served as the capital under the medieval Sultanate of Bengal and later as a prominent trading hub during the Mughal period. While the greater Sonargaon region boasts relics from as early as the 13th century, Panam Nagar specifically rose to prominence during the British rule, reflecting a blend of Mughal, Indo-European, and neoclassical architectural influences. Architectural Beauty Panam City consists of a single narrow street flanked by around 52 buildings, most of which are now in ruins. The buildings are typically two or three stories high, with ornate balconies, tall arched windows, intricate stucco work, and spacious courtyards. The architectural details reflect a mixture of Bengali craftsmanship and colonial finesse, with some influences of Greek revival elements. Each structure once served as a home, warehouse, or office space for its wealthy owners. Walking through the city today, one can still imagine the once-bustling street filled with traders, palanquins, and the sounds of life. Decline and Abandonment Panam City’s decline began in the early 20th century due to a combination of factors — political unrest, the partition of Bengal in 1947, communal tensions, and the gradual migration of Hindu families to India. By the 1960s, most of the city was abandoned. Over time, natural decay, lack of preservation, and occasional vandalism contributed to its ruined state. Cultural and Touristic Significance Today, Panam City is under the care of the Bangladesh Department of Archaeology and is recognized as a protected heritage site. It draws tourists, history enthusiasts, photographers, and researchers from across the country and abroad. The site is also close to the Folk Art and Craft Museum and the ancient Goaldi Mosque, enriching the visitor experience. Despite its historical and cultural importance, Panam City faces threats from urban encroachment, lack of funds for conservation, and environmental damage. Preservation efforts have been initiated, but more sustainable and community-driven approaches are needed to restore and protect this unique site. Final Thoughts Panam City is more than a collection of ruined mansions; it is a silent witness to Bangladesh’s colonial past, trade legacy, and changing demographics. As the country modernizes rapidly, preserving such heritage sites becomes essential to maintain a tangible connection to its multifaceted history. A walk through Panam is a walk through time — echoing stories of elegance, power, and eventual decline.

review_text_clean: How to get there and tips: It is located 25 kilometers North of Sylhet City in Gowainghat Upazila. There are more than one way to go to Bisnakandi. Tourists can use the Sylhet-Guainghat Road via the airport and take a left turn to reach Hadarpar from where a local boat may be hired to arrive at Bisnakandi. Visitors can go to Hadarpar by CNG-run auto-rickshaws, which are available for hire at Amberkhana Point in Sylhet city. It took us two and a half hour to reach there and one hour ten minutes to return. So you can imagine how important is your route selection. Although we did not regret as it was a beautiful scenic road. An alternative would be to go to Pangthumai first, and then hire a boat near Borhill Fall and ride along the branch of the Piyan which flows west towards Bisnakandi. The boat ride, which takes a little over an hour, on the sinuous river with lush green mountains on both sides is an unforgettable experience. To go to Bisanakandi only, the boat will charge 1,450 taka. For both Bisanakandi and Pantumai, they will charge 2,100 taka. The boat can accommodate up to 10 adults. Bisanakandi is located 315 km away from Dhaka. Bisanakandi is 25 km away from Sylhet. Alternative routs are 59 km and 66 km from the city center. As you will love to get yourself wet under the cold water for a long time and fight with the current and enjoy the view at Bisanakandi, I recommend to get started within 9:00 am in the morning from Sylhet. Bring a towel and extra clothing with you. You can take a morning flight to Sylhet and visit there as it is very close to the airport. I loved the place. Who ever loves travelling, must go there.

review_text_clean: Visited the M. A. G. Osmani Museum in Sylhet today, a place that quietly holds layers of personal and national history. The building itself, known as *Nur Monjil*, originally belonged to Osmani’s father. Following the death of General M. A. G. Osmani in 1984, the house was later converted into a museum around 1987. The structure consists of five rooms, two of which are used for administrative purposes, while the remaining three serve as exhibition spaces. The first room offers an intimate glimpse into his daily life, displaying personal items such as his bed, chairs, tables, clothing, a hanger, and a collection of photographs. The second room focuses more on his public and military life. It showcases medals, badges, and honors he received throughout his career as a Major General. Alongside these are pieces of furniture he used to host guests, as well as paintings by various artists depicting him and moments from the Liberation War. The final room brings together more of his personal and domestic life. Here, visitors can see another bed, a prayer mat, his personal work table, and a large room-sized map of Bangladesh that he reportedly used during the Liberation War. The room also includes his family dining space, an old refrigerator, dinnerware, and photographs from the later years of his life—some of which are in color, adding a different emotional texture to the experience. Entry tickets are quite affordable, costing only 20 BDT for Bangladeshi visitors, while foreign visitors are charged a higher fee. The staff members are knowledgeable and engaging, often interacting with visitors and sharing insights about Osmani’s life and contributions. The outdoor area is equally well maintained, with greenery that adds to the calm atmosphere. There is also a swing in the yard, along with a grave. According to the guard, the grave belongs to the original owner of the property. The Osmani family chose not to relocate it, preserving it as a mark of respect. Overall, the museum offers a thoughtful and grounded experience, connecting personal memory with the broader history of Bangladesh.

review_text_clean: Osmani Museum, Sylhet The Osmani Museum is named after Bangabir General Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani, the Commander-in-Chief of Bangladesh Forces (12 April 1971 – 7 April 1972) during the liberation war. It is situated at the heart of the Sylhet City Corporation area in the Sylhet Division of Bangladesh. It is about 12 km from the Sylhet Osmani International Airport and 3 km from the Sylhet Railway Station. Owned aoperated by the Bangladesh National Museum, this museum was established to pay rich tribute to the great hero of Bangladesh for his outstanding contributions in the liberation war of the country and founding the armed forces of Bangladesh. The foundation stone had been laid on 16 February 1985 and it was inaugurated on 4 March 1987 by the then president of Bangladesh H M Ershad. Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani also known as Bangabir (the Hero of Bengal) was born on 1 September 1918 in Sunamganj of Sylhet. He was the commander-in-chief of the Mukti Bahini during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War and was the first Bengali four star general. Osmani’s career spanned over five decades, beginning with his service in the British Indian Army in 1939. He fought in Burma during World War II, and served in the Pakistan Army until 1967. Osmani was appointed head of the Bengali armed resistance in 1971 by the Provisional Government of Bangladesh, and he is regarded as the founder of the Bangladesh Armed Forces. General Osmani retired in 1972. review_text_clean: Osmani Museum is a museum in Kotwali Thana of Sylhet, Bangladesh. The ancestors' home of Bangabir General Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani, the Commander-in-Chief of Bangladesh Forces (12 April 1971 – 7 April 1972) has been transformed into today's famous "Osmani Museum". It is situated at the heart (Dhopa Dighir Par) of the Sylhet City Corporation area in renowned Sylhet Division of Bangladesh. It is about 12 km from the Sylhet Osmani International Airport and 3 km from the Sylhet Railway Station. Maintained and organised by the Bangladesh National Museum, this museum has been established to pay rich tribute to the great hero of Bangladesh for his outstanding accomplishments. This will surely act as a stimulus to the future generations. The foundation stone was laid on 16 February 1985 and it was inaugurated on 4 March 1987 by the then president of Bangladesh H M Ershad. 1 Gallery 1 2 Gallery 2 3 Gallery 3 4 Relevant information Gallery 1 The entire room has been decorated with showpieces similar to a bedroom. There are four chairs made of cane and two centre tables, one simple wardrobe and one wooden bed with two side tables. The favourite wrist watch, which General Osmani wore till the last hours of his life; military stick, two briefcases, a telephone set, number of books and used crockery, are kept on one side. The other side is decorated with an Alana, which contains two suits, two uniforms (khaki and deep green), two shirts (white and light blue), two panjabi, a brown sleeveless coat, four pairs of shoes including one military boot, a black umbrella, brown colour well decorated walking stick. A round table and a wooden book shelf with many books and magazines from home and abroad including "Who's Who in the World" (editions: 1978–1979 and 1980–1981) are placed in a corner. Gallery 2 Decorated as a drawing room, there are few furniture made of cane, which includes chairs – four 1 sitter, one 3 sitter, one 2 sitter, a centre table, two side tables etc. First one contains the badges, medals, ranks of General and the passport of General Osmani. And the third one displays number of credentials, which includes the Certificate of Independence Award – 1985 along with the invitation card and brief biography of the award winners. One card contains the autograph of Mrs. Indira Gandhi of India along with envelop sent to General Osmani. Among them the important few are; General Osmani speaking to the audiences after the ceremonial guard of honour presented by the army on the occasion of the grand arrival of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 10 March 1971, landing at Sylhet airport in 1972, General Osmani with the sector commanders of the liberation war of Bangladesh, with acting president of Mujib Nagar government Syed Nazrul Islam, with president Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, with Shaheed president Ziaur Rahman, with ex president Ershad, with the martyrs family at the East Bengal Regimental Centre in 1981 etc. Gallery 3 A black reading table and chair, bed, prayer stand, Jaynamaz (Prayer Cloth), prayer cap etc. are lay down meticulously as exhibits. The other items include one black almirah, one fridge, dining table with six chairs, antique crockery and others. The operational map of Bangladesh (scale 1: 2,50,00), used by the General during the liberation war of Bangladesh, is also displayed in this room along with numerous credentials presented by the civil society. Relevant information Osmani Museum remains open every day except Thursday. From Sunday to Wednesday the timings is from 10:30 AM to 5:30 PM. On Friday and Saturday it remains open from 3:30 PM to 5:30 PM. The museum authority celebrates the birth (1 September) and death (16 February) anniversaries of General M A G Osmani along with the independent (26 March) and victory day (16 December) at the museum premises. Total 11 hard working individuals are taking proper care of this precious establishment.

review_text_clean: Foy’s Lake is a magnificent man-made reservoir located in the Khulshi area of Chattogram, Bangladesh, covering approximately 336 acres of picturesque hilly terrain. Originally excavated in 1924 under the supervision of British railway engineer Mr. Foy, the lake was initially designed to provide a steady water supply to the nearby Assam-Bengal Railway colony. Today, it has evolved into a premier tourist destination managed by the Concord Group, featuring a sprawling complex that includes the Foy’s Lake Concord Amusement World, Sea World Water Park, and luxury lakeside resorts. Visitors are drawn to the lake’s serene emerald waters, which are framed by lush green ridges like Asmani, Gagandwip, and Jaltungi, and the towering Batali Hill. The area is a biodiversity hotspot, home to various species of deer, rabbits, and over 15 species of birds, making it a haven for nature photographers and families alike. Adventure seekers can enjoy modern rides such as roller coasters and bumper boats, while those looking for tranquility can take scenic boat cruises across the 80-foot-deep waters. With its observation towers offering a bird’s-eye view of the port city and its dedicated picnic spots, Foy's Lake stands as a perfect blend of historical utility and modern recreation. You can find more details and plan your visit on the official Foy’s Lake Concord website.

In time, it became known as Foy’s Lake after the name of engineer Foy. There are also modern restaurants, merchandise shops, gift shops and Sea World Concord, the largest water park in the country. The lake’s water depth is a maximum of 78 to 80 feet and a minimum of 38 to 40 feet. For exclusive entertainment in Foy’s Lake, there are many international standard rides such as the Ferris Wheel, Family Roller Coaster, Bumper Car, Pirate Ship, Coffee Cup, Dry Slides, Circus Train, Pony Adventure, Baby Dragon, Baby Carousel, Circus Swing, Apollo Flight, Large Boats, Small Boats, Speed Boats, Paddle Boats, Racing Boats, Duck/Anchor Paddle Boats, Sampan and many more. In Foy’s Lake, there are – International standard accommodation facilities like Resorts, Bungalows, Honeymoon Chalets etc. Exclusive boats (Large Boat, Speed Boat, Paddle Boat, Sampan etc.) Air-conditioned Lake View Restaurants, Floating Restaurants along with Merchandise & Gift Shops. Arrangements for hiking & trekking in the hilly forests and access to the tall observation tower for the best scenic views.

review_text_clean: ​The Experience ​The park’s landscape is dominated by towering Sal trees (Shorea robusta), which create a dense, rhythmic canopy that stays green throughout the year. It feels like a "breathing lung" for the region. While it isn't a deep jungle, the 5,000+ hectares of forest provide a sense of wilderness that is hard to find elsewhere so close to the city. ​Key Highlights ​Nature Trails: The park features several walking paths that are excellent for light trekking. The terrain is a mix of flat land and low hillocks (locally called chalas), making it a manageable hike for all ages. ​Boating: There is a large excavated lake where you can rent pedal boats. It’s a peaceful way to see the forest from a different perspective. ​Wildlife: While large animals are rare now, you can still spot monkeys (rhesus macaques), various bird species (like the Brown Wood Owl), and occasionally deer in the mini-zoo area. ​Family & Picnics: With over 30 designated picnic spots and several rest houses, it is a top choice for family gatherings and corporate outings, especially during the winter months.

While it isn't a deep jungle, the 5,000+ hectares of forest provide a sense of wilderness that is hard to find elsewhere so close to the city. ​Key Highlights ​Nature Trails: The park features several walking paths that are excellent for light trekking. The terrain is a mix of flat land and low hillocks (locally called chalas), making it a manageable hike for all ages. ​Boating: There is a large excavated lake where you can rent pedal boats. It’s a peaceful way to see the forest from a different perspective. ​Wildlife: While large animals are rare now, you can still spot monkeys (rhesus macaques), various bird species (like the Brown Wood Owl), and occasionally deer in the mini-zoo area. ​Family & Picnics: With over 30 designated picnic spots and several rest houses, it is a top choice for family gatherings and corporate outings, especially during the winter months.

review_text_clean: Bhawal National Park is 40 km away from the capital Dhaka and has been developed in the shadow of Joydevpur in Gazipur. It is also known as Bhawal's Gajari Madha by many due to its abundance of Gajari trees. Spread over an area of about 5022 hectares, Bhawal National Park was recognized as a National Park in 1982. Among the 221 species of plants in the park are 43 species of trees, 19 species of shrubs, 3 species of palms, 27 species of grasses, 24 species of vines and 104 species of medicinal plants. There are also 64 different species of animals including 13 species of mammals, 9 species of reptiles, 5 species of birds and amphibians. Many people organize picnics and various events in this park, full of natural beauty and biodiversity. Entering through gate number 3 of Bhawal Garh, the first thing you will notice are the two elephant sculptures at the terracotta entrance. Inside the park there are 31 picnic spots, 19 beautiful cottages, state-of-the-art rest houses, butterfly garden, turtle breeding center and children's park. If you are tired of walking among the rows of trees in the garden, there are benches or canopies for rest. Green paddy fields, ponds or small lakes can be seen in the midst of this extensive forest. Along with a boat ride on the lake, there is a towering watch tower to view the entire park. The distance between Gazipur Sadar and Bhawal Ghazari, ie Bhawal National Park, is only 3 km. After crossing the Jaidebpur intersection and moving a little further, the main entrance of Bhawal Garh will be noticed on the right hand side. You can go to Bhawal Udyan by your own car from Dhaka or by any bus bound for Mymensingh from Mahakhali, Airport or Rajendrapur Chowrasta via Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway. Everyone is invited to see this beauty of nature.

review_text_clean: Ratargul Swamp Forest is one of the most magical natural spots I’ve visited in Bangladesh. Just about 26 km from Sylhet city, this freshwater swamp forest offers a rare and serene escape — especially during the monsoon season when much of the forest is submerged under water. Riding through the flooded channels with trees like koroch, hijal, and kadam rising out of the water feels like entering another world. What I loved: The boat ride through narrow waterways was peaceful and beautiful. You glide under green canopies, past reflective water, and listen to bird calls — it’s calming. Lots of plant diversity. Trees like Pongamia pinnata (koroch), Murta (Schumannianthus dichotoma), Hijal (Barringtonia acutangula), Kadam etc. give the forest a rich green texture that changes with the season. Birdlife & wildlife. I saw kingfishers, egrets, some monkeys, snakes, small water‐birds. If you go in winter or during migration, there are even more species. The watchtower gives a nice overview of the forest canopy. A good spot for photos. What could be better: Littering is a problem. Plastic bottles, food wrappers, even floating trash sometimes, which spoils the beauty and might harm the wildlife. Too many tourists sometimes — especially on weekends, holidays, and during peak season. This crowding creates noise, disturbs animals and birds, and puts stress on the forest environment. Facilities are minimal. There are no places to stay inside the forest, limited shelter if it rains, few places to rest, etc. If you plan a long trip, good preparation is needed. Tips: Visit in the monsoon season (June-October) for the full submerged-forest experience. But be ready for water, rain, mosquitoes. Hire a boat and a local guide — guides know good spots, the right paths, and can help avoid disturbances. Bring snacks, water, rain gear, and insect repellent. Try to avoid peak times (weekends, holidays) for a quieter, more immersive experience. --- Overall, Ratargul is one of Bangladesh’s natural gems. It offers an unforgettable feeling of being in a “forest on water,” somewhere in the intersection of the wild and peaceful. If conservation and respectful tourism are maintained (and waste managed better), I think it can remain a wonder for many visitors to come.

review_text_clean: On June 1st, 2025, we had the incredible opportunity to visit Ratargul Swamp Forest in Sylhet, Bangladesh—and the experience was beyond words. Known as the only freshwater swamp forest in the country, Ratargul is a place where nature breathes in its rawest form. But what made my visit even more magical was the weather that day. It was raining, and with the occasional lightning illuminating the sky, the entire forest transformed into something surreal—almost mythical. As we approached the forest, clouds loomed low and heavy. The earthy scent of wet leaves and soil filled the air. We boarded a small wooden boat, and the moment we entered the swamp area, I felt like I had stepped into a dream. The rain gently pattered on the canopy above us, occasionally breaking through and splashing on our faces. It wasn’t heavy enough to be a nuisance—just the right kind to make the entire journey feel more cinematic. Each drop added to the melody of the forest. The trees, mostly Koroch and Hijol, stood tall and majestic with their trunks submerged in calm water, giving off reflections that shimmered and rippled with every movement of the boat. Rainwater mingled with the swamp, enhancing the sense of immersion and purity. It was so quiet, yet so alive. The only sounds were the splash of oars, raindrops on leaves, and distant thunder rolling through the hills of Sylhet. Then came the lightning. Every few minutes, a flash of light would streak across the sky, briefly illuminating the entire forest in a cold, electric blue. For those few seconds, everything stood still—the trees, the water, the sky—and I could see the entire swamp lit up like a painting. It wasn’t scary; it was powerful, beautiful, and humbling. Nature was putting on a light show, and we were just lucky enough to witness it. The contrast between the soft rain and the sharp lightning created a rhythm that made the boat ride feel like something out of a fantasy novel. Despite the rain, or perhaps because of it, the views were astonishing. Every turn in the narrow waterways revealed new corners of the forest, each more photogenic than the last. Some trees bent over the water, their branches dipping gently in. Others stood alone, noble and silent, their trunks covered in moss. Occasionally, we spotted birds darting through the rain, unfazed, adding even more life to the scenery. The rain also brought out the colors of the forest in a way that sunlight couldn’t. The greens were richer, deeper, almost glowing. The water appeared darker, creating stunning reflections. It was hard to put the camera down, but even harder not to just sit and absorb the moment. The experience wasn’t just visual—it was emotional. It made me feel small in the best way, like I was just a quiet observer in a world that existed long before me. Ratargul, in the rain, during lightning, is something you have to experience to truly understand. It’s peaceful, mysterious, and absolutely beautiful. Whether you're a nature lover, a photographer, or someone just looking to escape the noise of city life, this place will leave you spellbound. review_text_clean: Ratargul Swamp Forest, located in Gowainghat Upazila of Sylhet, Bangladesh, is a rare and enchanting freshwater swamp forest, often referred to as the "Amazon of Bangladesh." Covering approximately 3,325 acres, with 504 acres designated as a wildlife sanctuary, it stands as one of the few freshwater swamp forests in the world. During the monsoon season, from June to October, the forest transforms dramatically as water levels rise between 20 to 30 feet, submerging the forest floor and creating a surreal landscape where trees appear to float on water. Navigating through the forest by boat offers a unique and immersive experience, allowing visitors to witness the rich biodiversity up close. The forest is home to over 70 plant species, including the dominant koroch (Pongamia pinnata) and hijal (Barringtonia acutangula) trees, and supports a diverse array of wildlife, such as monkeys, otters, and numerous bird species, including the endangered masked finfoot . Accessing Ratargul is relatively straightforward. From Sylhet city, travelers can hire a CNG auto-rickshaw to reach the forest, with fares ranging from 800 to 1,200 BDT for a round trip . Boat rentals are available at designated ghats, costing between 700 to 800 BDT for a two-hour journey through the forest's waterways . While the forest's beauty is undeniable, visitors should be mindful of certain precautions. The area is home to various wildlife, including snakes and leeches, especially during the monsoon. It's advisable to wear life jackets, avoid touching submerged vegetation, and refrain from littering to preserve the forest's pristine condition . In summary, Ratargul Swamp Forest offers a unique and tranquil escape into nature's embrace. Its serene waterways, rich biodiversity, and ethereal beauty make it a must-visit destination for nature enthusiasts and adventure seekers alike.

review_text_clean: Jaflong is a stunningly beautiful destination located in the Sylhet division of northeastern Bangladesh, right on the border with the Indian state of Meghalaya. Known for its crystal-clear river, rolling hills, and views of the Khasi mountain range, Jaflong is one of the most scenic spots in the country and a favorite among nature lovers and photographers. The main attraction is the Dawki River (locally known as the Piyain River), whose transparent turquoise water is so clear that boats appear to float in the air. Visitors often take boat rides to explore the riverbanks, waterfalls, and the surrounding landscapes, which offer an almost surreal natural experience. During winter, the water is especially clear, and the stone beds beneath the surface are perfectly visible. Jaflong is also culturally fascinating. It’s home to the Khasi indigenous community, and visitors can explore traditional Khasi villages, experience their way of life, and even visit a unique betel leaf garden. The area is also known for stone collection, and while the manual labor seen here is intense, it’s a powerful reflection of local livelihoods. Surrounded by tea gardens, forests, and misty hills, Jaflong offers a peaceful and refreshing break from urban life. With increasing accessibility and improved tourist facilities, it is quickly becoming one of Bangladesh’s most popular eco-tourism destinations.

review_text_clean: The Sylhet Agricultural University and Sylhet Engineering College are both close to the Tilagarh Ecopark, which is located in a reserve forest. Locals refer to the location as "Aloor Tol - আলুর তল" frequently. There used to be virtually limited access to the large forest and an extremely dense forest. The area's unaltered, naturally created forest with tree canopies and hillocks was a favorite among locals. The environment used to drastically change as soon as you arrived at the Aloor Tol region. The gorgeous dense forest with a variety of mature trees and hillocks becomes more and more engulfing the deeper you go. The government has since shown interest in it and taken action to protect this exceptional biodiverse forest. In 2006, Tilagarh Eco Parks were built on 112 acres of woodland. The Sylhet Forest Department, Ministry of Environment and Forest, is responsible for this ecopark initiative. An eco park's primary goals include the preservation and development of nearly extinct and rare plant species, the protection and enhancement of current plant and animal life, the breeding and advancement of indigenous plant species through integrated management, the preservation of the local environment and the socioeconomic advancement of the local populace, the growth of the planned ecotourism sector, and the provision of opportunities for study and research. Nine ecoparks have been established by the Department of Forest in different parts of Bangladesh, taking into account their unique natural features and characteristics including location. These include the Bashkhali Ecopark, the Madhavkundo Ecopark, the Madhutila Ecopark, the Sitakunda Botanical Garden and Ecopark, the Tilagarh Ecopark, the Jafflong Garden Park, and the Barshijora Ecopark. "Numerous species of animals can be spotted in the wild at Tilagarh Ecopark. Foxes, monkeys, jackel, rabbits, pandas, Mathura (Chrysolophus), entellus, and other animals are among them. Additionally, you can find Mayna, parakeets, doves, Haridas, and other varieties of birds here." Tilagarh Eco Park makes it possible to appreciate the natural beauty of the jungles and learn about their ecology firsthand, which contributes to raising public awareness of the importance of preserving bio-diversity. Unfortunately, Tilagarh Eco Park utterly failed to raise awareness of bio-diversity of the Eco Park among the general people. The relevant information about the Eco Park is not provided by even a single interpretation display board or information location! Additionally, it has failed to maintain its individuality and natural attractiveness! The beauty and authenticity of this incredible biodiverse ecosystem are currently being hampered by the presence of numerous residential units, government office buildings, college campuses, and universities. In the park, there is a restroom, a picnic area, and a kids' area. These are intended to be, after all. Children's Corner needs urgent repairs because it is now unfit for kids. In an effort to boost tourism in Sylhet and increase the number of visitors, the government built a wildlife conservation centre in the Tilagarh Eco Park in 2018. The Wildlife Conservation Centre was constructed carelessly, which is bad for the Eco Park. Animal sightings are quite rare at the Wildlife Conservation Centre! You must pay to see this natural beauty; entry to the environmental park is not free.

review_text_clean: There is some confusion on the names. Tilagarh Eco Park is merely a road through a forest that charges you an entrance fee. It has a small fenced area for it two zebras, and another for it snakes. It has small cages for its two mccaws and two parrots. (Here you may see a free monkey hoping for a handout.) Now the park has a decent trail that I was keen to walk on. But as I started, a group of three men (including a policeman) told me to stay on the road, the only place in the park I didn't want to be. Now five km north is Khadimnagar National Park. It is a ruse. On the map it is a large protected area. But the reality is only about 50 acres of somewhat protected walking trail. Tea is growing everywhere else. And bamboo is harvested as needed by the villages in the national park. Walking for 12 km in the park the only mammals I encountered were domestic ones and a squirrel. The foreigners are charged $5.75 for entry. Locals about $0.25. Coming here for birds? Don't. Black drongo, whiskered and red-vented bulbuls, tailorbirds, cattle egret, little else.

review_text_clean: Visited Lawachara National Park in Sreemangal (Kamalganj), which is often described as a "living botanical garden" due to its incredible diversity of plant species with family. It is basically a wild forest housing diverse species of plants and wildlife. Lawachara is a semi-evergreen tropical rainforest approximately 1,250 hectares & houses over 167 species of plants. The forest canopy is dominated by trees like Garjan (Dipterocarpus which can grow up to 70 meters tall, as well as Teak, Jarul, and Lohakat. It is also famous for its orchid diversity, with more than 100 recorded species. It is situated about 8–10 km from Sreemangal, best to travel by micro bus or CNG autos. The forest is at its most "botanical" and lush during the monsoon (June–August). For a wild, natural botanical experience, Lawachara is considered the best in the country.

It’s easily one of the most photogenic spots in Sreemangal. 🌿 What to Expect * The Vibe: Dense canopy, towering trees, and a surprisingly cool microclimate even when the sun is out. * Wildlife: If you’re lucky (and quiet!), you’ll spot the Hoolock Gibbons. Their calls are the soundtrack of the forest. I also saw some vibrant butterflies and rare birds that made for incredible macro shots. * The Famous Tracks: The train line passing through the forest is iconic. It’s the ultimate "Instagrammable" spot, but please stay alert for trains while snapping your photos! 📸 Photography Tips * Lighting: The sun filters through the leaves in "god rays" during the early morning (7:00 AM – 9:00 AM). This is the best time for that ethereal forest glow. * Gear: Bring a zoom lens if you’re a birdwatcher; the Gibbons stay high up in the canopy. * Stability: It can get a bit dim under the thick cover, so keep your hand steady or use a higher ISO to avoid blurry shots. 💡 Pro-Tips for Visitors * Hire a Guide: It’s affordable and worth it. They know exactly where the animals hide and can lead you through the three different hiking trails (half-hour, one-hour, and three-hour treks). * Leech Alert: If you go during the rainy season, wear long socks and carry some salt or lime. They are harmless but very persistent! * Respect Nature: Please don't leave any plastic behind. Let's keep this green lung of Bangladesh pristine. Summary: A peaceful, lush escape that feels like stepping into a National Geographic documentary. Perfectly accessible for families but rugged enough for solo adventurers.

review_text_clean: Lawachara National Park, located in Kamalganj upazila of Moulvibazar district, is a protected forest area in Bangladesh. Nature has generously bestowed its beauty here. Various species of trees and diverse wild animals such as deer, monkeys, different species of snakes, jungle fowl, and fishing cats can be found in the park. It is a tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forest with an area of 1,250 hectares. One scene of the famous movie “Around the World in 80 Days,” based on Jules Verne’s renowned novel, was shot in this forest. The railway that runs through the forest was the location for that particular scene. The scene shows a train rushing through the forest. Suddenly, the driver notices a herd of elephants leisurely walking across the tracks. The train stops. The protagonist, David Niven, steps out to investigate. A ritual of Sati was happening in a nearby village, and the hero rushes to save the girl—Shirley MacLaine. This scene was filmed in the railway area of Lawachara. Biodiversity Lawachara National Park is home to 167 species of plants including teak, chapalish, agar, and raktan. There are 4 species of amphibians, 6 species of reptiles, 246 species of birds, and 20 species of mammals. Bangladesh’s only living African teak tree is located in this park. The endangered gibbon, found in only four countries in the world, has its largest population in Bangladesh at Lawachara. There are about 276 species of wildlife here including pangolins, pythons, and many types of birds. Inside the park is the centuries-old Khasia Punji, a tribal village that preserves its unique culture and heritage. Visiting Lawachara The park offers three hiking trails of different lengths—30 minutes, 1 hour, and 3 hours—allowing visitors to experience nature up close. These trails are designed to avoid disturbing the environment, and a variety of insects, plants, birds, and orchids can be seen. Lucky visitors might even spot monkeys or gibbons. Both local and foreign tourists visit Lawachara year-round, with winter being the most popular season. 30-Minute Trail: This trail starts on the left after crossing the railway line. High in the trees, one may see Capped langurs. The path leads through dense forest, offering a peaceful and thrilling experience. Wild orchids can be seen on the tall tree branches, although this may not be their blooming season. The trail loops back to its starting point. 1-Hour Trail: This trail begins with the massive Gandharui tree, also known as Kasturi, believed to have a fragrance used in perfumes. Along this path are trees like jhawa, jagdumur, mooli bamboo, kathali chapa, and leha. Old chapalish and gamari trees are also found here. The fruits of various fig trees attract gibbons, monkeys, and many other wild animals. If you're lucky, you might see a barking deer or jungle fowl. 3-Hour Trail: This adventurous trail passes the Magurchhara Punji, a Khasi village where the residents primarily cultivate betel leaves. The village was established by the Forest Department in the 1950s. Along the trail are large bamboo groves inhabited by Capped langurs and rare slow lorises, which are nocturnal and usually sleep during the day in bamboo clusters. Various bird species are also seen along the way, and towards the end, one might spot gibbons—Lawachara’s main attraction—which live high in the trees in groups. Entry Fees Adults: 20 BDT Students and minors: 10 BDT Foreigners: 5 USD or equivalent in BDT Parking (cars, jeeps, microbuses): 25 BDT Guides: 200–600 BDT based on category Picnic spot: 10 BDT per person

Both local and foreign tourists visit Lawachara year-round, with winter being the most popular season. 30-Minute Trail: This trail starts on the left after crossing the railway line. High in the trees, one may see Capped langurs. The path leads through dense forest, offering a peaceful and thrilling experience. Wild orchids can be seen on the tall tree branches, although this may not be their blooming season. The trail loops back to its starting point. 1-Hour Trail: This trail begins with the massive Gandharui tree, also known as Kasturi, believed to have a fragrance used in perfumes. Along this path are trees like jhawa, jagdumur, mooli bamboo, kathali chapa, and leha. Old chapalish and gamari trees are also found here. The fruits of various fig trees attract gibbons, monkeys, and many other wild animals. If you're lucky, you might see a barking deer or jungle fowl. 3-Hour Trail: This adventurous trail passes the Magurchhara Punji, a Khasi village where the residents primarily cultivate betel leaves. The village was established by the Forest Department in the 1950s. Along the trail are large bamboo groves inhabited by Capped langurs and rare slow lorises, which are nocturnal and usually sleep during the day in bamboo clusters. Various bird species are also seen along the way, and towards the end, one might spot gibbons—Lawachara’s main attraction—which live high in the trees in groups. The meticulously preserved forest provides abundant opportunities for trekking and jungle walks, allowing visitors to encounter over 460 different species of birds, mammals, and reptiles, including deer, wild chickens, squirrels, pythons, endangered hoolock gibbons, capped langurs, slow lorises, birds, snakes, banana spiders, and more. Nature enthusiasts can immerse themselves in the lush surroundings and close proximity to wildlife by exploring the numerous trails within the forest. Situated in the northeastern region of Bangladesh, Lawachara National Park is a significant nature reserve located in Kamalganj Upazila, Maulvi Bazar District, encompassing the West Bhanugach Reserved Forest spanning 2,740 hectares (27.4 km2). The park, covering approximately 1,250 hectares (12.5 km2) of semi-evergreen and mixed deciduous forests, was designated as a national park by the Bangladesh government on July 7, 1996, under the Wildlife Act of 1974. *How to Reach* Travel from Dhaka to Kamalapur or the Airport Railway Station to Srimangal, Moulvibazar Railway Station via Upban, Jayantika, Parabat, or Kalni Express Train. Alternatively, take a bus from Dhaka to Fakirapul or Saidabad, using Hanif Enterprise, Shyamoli Paribahan, Sylhet Express, ENA, etc., non-AC buses to Srimangal, Moulvibazar. Srimangal can also be reached by bus or train from Chittagong. Trains like Paharika and Udayan Express run six days a week from Chittagong to Srimangal. Lawachara Rain Forest is located 30 km from Moulvibazar district town. Lawachara National Park is a haven for nature lovers. Its lush greenery and diverse wildlife provide a perfect blend of adventure and tranquility. The park boasts remarkable biodiversity, with various bird species and primates making each step a thrilling exploration. The Canopy Walkway offers an exhilarating experience, providing a unique perspective of the forest canopy. Well-maintained trails cater to both novice and experienced hikers, offering opportunities to spot elusive Hoolock Gibbons and other captivating creatures. Friendly and helpful park staff enhance the overall experience, making it a must-visit for those seeking a glimpse of Bangladesh's extraordinary natural beauty. My visit to Lawachara was a fantastic experience. Considered one of the largest national parks in Bangladesh, it showcases numerous rare species of trees, animals, and insects. Walking through the forest, you'll notice a significant drop in temperature, especially during winter. The train line running through the forest adds to the scenic ambiance, making it a delightful sight. Despite being a peaceful forest, maintaining it requires considerable effort. Unfortunately, visitors sometimes disturb the natural animals by throwing stones and shouting, and authorities often fail to address this issue. The presence of a busy rail line within the forest poses a threat to animals, as they are sometimes killed by fast-moving trains. In conclusion, Lawachara is a must-visit destination for nature enthusiasts, offering a captivating experience amidst its diverse flora and fauna. Khan Abdul Latif

review_text_clean: Lawachara National Sanctuary Forest, located in the heart of Moulvibazar, is one of Bangladesh’s most ecologically significant and biologically diverse tropical rainforests. Home to endangered species such as the Hoolock Gibbons, rare birds, amphibians, and countless plant species, this sanctuary is not only a vital habitat for wildlife but also a national treasure that represents our country’s natural heritage. However, my recent visit to Lawachara was far from pleasing. Despite its significance, the forest is suffering due to human negligence and lack of proper regulation. The sanctuary was overcrowded with visitors, many of whom seemed unaware—or unconcerned—about the rules of a protected forest area. I witnessed people littering freely: plastic bags, chips packets, and other non-biodegradable waste scattered across the forest floor, often outside designated disposal areas. Even worse, visitors were making loud noises, playing music, and even mimicking the calls of the Hoolock Gibbons, disturbing the already vulnerable wildlife. The sheer volume of people and noise made it feel like the forest was no longer a sanctuary for animals, but rather a playground for a careless crowd. Such behavior not only disrupts the peace of the forest but also poses a direct threat to its delicate ecosystem. Moreover, there is a regional road and a railway line that pass through the forest, with no green bridges or wildlife crossings in place. The high flow of traffic puts the animals at constant risk and fragments their habitat, further endangering their survival. Authorities must act immediately. Entry to the forest should be more strictly regulated, with a limited number of visitors allowed at a time. Educational signage and staff should be present to ensure rules are followed. Most importantly, infrastructure such as green bridges must be built over roads and railways to allow safe animal movement. Lawachara is not just a travel destination—it’s a living, breathing ecosystem vital to the health of our planet. If immediate steps are not taken to protect it, we risk losing a crucial piece of Bangladesh’s natural identity and contributing to the ongoing destruction of our environment. Let us not forget: preserving nature is preserving ourselves.

review_text_clean: Transportation Bus or auto rickshaw can be used to reach this tourist destination. Details Ethnological museum is one of the most visited sites of Chattogram city. This museum is basically established to give a conception of the succession of various cultural groups of the country and their lifestyles. It is one of the two ethnological museums in the continent of Asia and the other is in Japan. It also comes to help in research work. The museum was established on 1.25 acres of land adjacent to Badamtali of Agrabad Commercial area of Chattogram city in 1965. Since its inception, it is opened for visitors. History: The Department of Archeology, Bangladesh took the initiative for the establishment of the museum in 1965. The museum was opened in 1974 for public inspection. Later, between 1985 and 1995, two rooms were included in the museum. Yusuf Ali, the first education minister of the Government of Bangladesh inaugurated this museum on January 9, 1974. Description: The museum authorities have collected some rare materials used in the daily life of various cultural groups. Most of the materials are at risk of extinction. This museum has made comparative analysis of 25 small ethnic groups of Bangladesh with the ethnic groups of 5 foreign countries, in terms of various materials used by them. Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Mrung, Bawm, Khyang, Khumi, Chak, Rakhine, Pankhoa in the Chittagong Hill Tracts; Khasia, Manipuri, Pangan, Patra in Sylhet region; Garo, Hajong, Dalu, Mandai, Cooch in Mymensingh region; Santal, Oraon, Rajbangshi, Polia in Rajshahi-Dinajpur region; and Buno, Bagdi in the Jashore-Jhenaidah region are included in the small ethnic groups of Bangladesh. It has 4 galleries and 1 hall. The 3 galleries of the museum have arrangements for displaying various materials of 25 cultural groups of Bangladesh such as weapons, flower vases, clothes, boats, scissors, ornaments, bamboo pipes. The other gallery is used to show the life style of some communities in India, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan, Australia and Germany. Visitors get the chance to be acquainted with various festivals and culture of tribal people through maps and graffiti in the hall room. A part of the Berlin Wall of Germany, broken in 1989, is also displayed here. There is a garden in front of the museum. Visiting Information: Ethnological museum of Chattogram is open to visitors every day except Sunday and public holidays. According to the museum authorities, the museum receives 200-300 visitors daily including local and foreign researchers.

review_text_clean: I recently visited Patenga Sea Beach, and while it remains a popular landmark, the experience was a bit of a mixed bag. If you are planning a trip, here is a detailed breakdown of what to expect: ​The Atmosphere & Visuals ​The first thing you notice is that the beach has lost much of its natural, rugged charm. Due to the extensive use of concrete blocks and embankments for tide protection, the shoreline feels quite artificial. While these structures make it easier to walk around, they take away from the "wild" coastal beauty one usually expects from a sea beach. ​Crowds and Commercialization ​The area is heavily commercialized. There is an overwhelming number of street stalls and vendors lining the walkways. While it’s convenient if you want a quick snack or a souvenir, the sheer density of these shops makes the environment feel cluttered and disorganized. Unfortunately, this high volume of foot traffic and commerce has led to noticeable pollution; litter is common, which significantly detracts from the aesthetic appeal of the promenade. ​The "Sea Vibe" ​If you are looking for a place to sit in quiet contemplation and listen to the waves, you might be disappointed. Because of the noise, the crowds, and the industrial backdrop of the nearby port, the authentic sea vibe is largely missing. It feels more like a busy city park that happens to be next to water rather than a serene coastal escape. ​Family Suitability ​On a positive note, it is a functional spot for a family outing. The well-paved walkways are accessible for children and the elderly, and there are plenty of food options (like the famous spicy crab fry) to keep a group entertained. It’s a safe, easy-to-reach location for a quick afternoon hang-out. ​Final Verdict ​Patenga is worth a visit if you are already in Chattogram and want a convenient place to see the water with your family. However, if you are a nature lover seeking a pristine beach experience, the artificial layout and environmental clutter might leave you wanting more. It’s a great place for a stroll and a snack, but don’t expect a traditional "hidden gem" beach atmosphere.

Located about 14 kilometers south of Chattogram city center, it sits precisely at the unique geographical confluence where the Karnaphuli River meets the massive waters of the Bay of Bengal.Unlike the secluded and raw mangrove beaches of Sitakunda, Patenga is fully integrated into the city infrastructure, offering a lively festive atmosphere, highly accessible modern roads, and scenic maritime views.🌟 Key HighlightsThe Modern Promenade: The beach features a highly developed coastal walkway protected by thousands of massive concrete blocks and geobags. Bus fare is roughly 30 to 50 BDT.Alternatively, a private CNG auto-rickshaw or app-based ride-sharing car from the city center directly to the beach costs between 300 to 500 BDT.

review_text_clean: Guliakhali Sea Beach is located in Sitakunda Upazila of Chattogram district. Locally, it is known as Muradpur Beach. The beach is only 5 kilometers away from Sitakunda Bazar. Nature has spared no effort in beautifying the stunning Guliakhali Sea Beach. On one side, there is the vast expanse of the sea, and on the other, a Keora forest that makes this beach truly unique. You can see the breathing roots of the Keora trees along the canals that flow through the forest, which extends deep into the sea. This area offers an environment similar to that of a swamp forest or mangrove forest. What sets Guliakhali Beach apart is its wide carpet of green grass. The open green field beside the sea will surely soothe your eyes. Naturally formed winding canals run through the grassy area, which fill with water during high tide. The sight of these small water-filled canals surrounded by lush greenery is sure to enchant anyone. Since this beach is relatively unknown, there are fewer visitors, offering a quiet and serene atmosphere. Though the sea here may not be loud or wild with waves, the tranquil environment of Guliakhali Beach will give you a different kind of experience. If you wish, you can take a boat ride into the sea with the local fishermen. In that case, you will need to negotiate and fix the price beforehand. There are beautiful fields here—if you bring a football, it will feel like playing on a turf. A boat ride into the sea costs around 2000 BDT. If you want to camp, you can stay overnight by bringing your own tent.

review_text_clean: Guliakhali Sea Beach (also known as Muradpur Beach) is a unique coastal destination located in Sitakunda Upazila, Chattogram, Bangladesh. Unlike standard sandy beaches, it features a distinct ecosystem where a mangrove forest meets a vast carpet of lush green grass intersected by natural, winding water channels.Key HighlightsThe Landscape: It offers a swamp forest-like environment filled with Keora trees and visible breathing roots. Naturally formed ditches and narrow canals run across the grass, filling up beautifully during high tide.Tranquil Atmosphere: It is much less commercialized than Cox's Bazar, making it a peaceful getaway ideal for photography, catching stunning sunsets, and nature exploration.Best Time to Visit: The monsoon and post-monsoon seasons (June to October) highlight the most vibrant shades of green grass and fully filled canals. Early mornings or late afternoons are recommended to avoid midday heat and enjoy the sunset.How to Get ThereGuliakhali is located roughly 5 kilometers west of Sitakunda Bazar.Reach Sitakunda: Take any Chattogram-bound bus or train from Dhaka or other major cities and drop off at the Sitakunda Bazar intersection.Local Transport: Rent a local CNG auto-rickshaw from Sitakunda Bazar to the beach embankment (locally called the Beribadh). A shared ride costs around 30 to 40 BDT per person, while a reserved vehicle ranges from 150 to 200 BDT.Reaching the Shore: From the embankment drop-off, you must walk through a muddy trail to reach the main beach area. If you arrive during a high tide, local fishermen offer short boat transfers across the flooded terrain for roughly 30 BDT per person.
