review_text_clean: The Bangladesh Betar Transmission Centre at Kalurghat in Chittagong has turned into a 'Mini Bangladesh' under the project titled 'Shaheed Zia Smriti Complex'. Giving visitors a glimpse of rich historical background and heritage, life of people and their different cultures, flora and fauna of Bangladesh is the main objective behind the concept of 'Mini Bangladesh'. The prime minister, Khaleda Zia, is scheduled to inaugurate the Shaheed Zia Smriti Complex through a colorful ceremony on August 29 during her daylong visit to the port city. A source in the construction firm said all development works of the Smriti Complex have completed. The Smriti Complex has been built to keep the memory and various aspects of the glorious war of independence afresh in the minds of people, particularly the future generations through preserving and developing the historic site properly. The Concord Engineering and Construction Ltd has implemented the project under the supervision of the Public Works Department. The ministry of liberation war affairs had undertaken the scheme involving Tk 55.92 crore. The main feature of the Smriti Complex includes a big size fountain and a replica of Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban at the centre of a huge water body, a colorfully adorned spacious entrance, an over 200 feet high tower with stairs, elevators and modern restaurants, a public park, a long tunnel for monorail track, three rail station buildings keeping similarity with the Church of Saint Nicholas at Gazipur, Choto Sona Mosque and Baro Khuiti in Rajshahi, replicas of Carzon Hall, National Monument at Savar, Lalbagh Fort, Ahsan Manjil, Paharpur Monastery and homes of different tribal people in the country. Besides, the work of other amusement facilities, including rides such as a number of food kiosks, family coasters, ferries wheels, 12 horses carousel, paddle boats and kiddies swing, are also completed, sources said.

This clock was made by Ali Amjad's estate fund to honor him. Therefore the clock is known as Ali Amjad's Clock. The clock bell could be heard from far beyond the city. During the War of Liberation in 1971, this ancient Clock house was destroyed by the Pakistan army. After independence, Sylhet municipality reactivated the clock by repairing, but soon after the clock was stopped. In 1987 it was repaired and restored again. Since then the clock has been repaired and modified many times. And lastly, in 2011, Sylhet City Corporation repaired the clock again and it is now functioning properly. This is a must visit monument in Sylhet for the tourists interested in history.

review_text_clean: Located in Sylhet Sadar Upazila on the banks of the Surma River, this clock has a diameter of two and a half feet and a clock hand of two feet long. When clocks were not in free circulation, at that time, i.e. in 1874, this historic clock house was built on the banks of the Surma River on the right side of the Keen Bridge, the entrance to Sylhet city (North Surma), by Ali Ahmed Khan, the landlord of Pritthimpasha, Kulaura, Sylhet, in the name of his son Ali Amjad. The clock house, which has a high dome-shaped architectural style with corrugated iron on iron poles, has since become known as Ali Amjad's clock house. This ancient clock house was destroyed by the shelling of the invading forces during the Liberation War. After independence, the Sylhet Municipality repaired the clock and made it operational, but within a few days the clock hands stopped working. In 1987, Ali Amjad's clock was repaired and restarted. After the clock was restarted, craftsmen from a Dhaka company arranged for a remote control to keep the clock running. The clock's hands used to turn from the office of the municipal chairman through remote control. But within two to four years, the clock's hands stopped again. Then the clock was restarted electronically by the Sizan company. But within a year, the clock's hands stopped again. review_text_clean: If you’re visiting Sylhet and want to connect with the region’s rich culture and history, the Hasan Raja Museum is a must-see. Located just beside the famous Panshi Restaurant, this hidden gem offers a truly memorable experience that blends music, history, and spirituality. The museum is set in an old, charming house that once belonged to Hasan Raja’s family. Hasan Raja (1854–1922) was not only a respected zamindar but also one of Bengal’s most beloved mystic poets and folk singers. His songs, filled with deep emotions, love for nature, and spiritual wisdom, still touch people’s hearts today. Inside the museum, you’ll find a wide range of items that bring his story to life: • His personal belongings, such as clothes, household items, and zamindari records, give a peek into how he lived. • Handwritten manuscripts of his songs and poems reveal his powerful thoughts and philosophies. • Traditional musical instruments and recordings of his timeless folk songs let you experience the soul of his music. • Historical photos and family portraits make the visit feel more personal and real. The building itself reflects a mix of traditional Bengali and colonial architecture, adding to the unique atmosphere. Many visitors say the peaceful surroundings and old-style charm create a space that feels both reflective and inspiring. The museum also shares stories of the Raja family’s role in the cultural and social life of Sylhet, especially during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Whether you’re a student, a researcher, or just someone curious about Sylhet’s past, this museum offers plenty to explore and learn. Though the museum is generally well-kept, a few areas could benefit from more restoration. Still, it’s a beautiful place worth visiting. The entry fee is very affordable, making it open to all. And here’s a tip: don’t leave without listening to the recordings of Hasan Raja’s songs—hearing his voice and words brings everything to life in a magical way. Right next to Panshi Restaurant and easy to reach from anywhere in Sylhet city, the Hasan Raja Museum is more than just a tourist spot—it’s a place where you feel the spirit of a man who shaped Bengali folk music and poetry. Whether you’re into history, music, or simply looking for something meaningful to do in Sylhet, this museum should definitely be on your list.

The museum preserves his memory and showcases his contributions to Bengali folk music and poetry. The museum features a diverse array of artifacts, documents, and memorabilia associated with Hasan Raja: Items like his clothes, utensils, and zamindari records give visitors a glimpse into his lifestyle. Manuscripts of his poems and songs are displayed, showing the depth of his philosophical and spiritual thoughts. Exhibits include musical instruments and records of his timeless folk songs, which continue to inspire musicians and poets across generations. The museum also provides insights into the Raja family’s history, including their role in the socio-economic and cultural development of the region. Historical photographs and portraits of Hasan Raja and his family add a personal touch to the narrative. The museum itself is a blend of traditional and colonial-era architecture, reflecting the cultural essence of Sylhet. Visitors often find the ambiance calm and reflective, making it a perfect space to connect with the mysticism of Hasan Raja's works. review_text_clean: The predecessor's home of Hason Raja has been transformed into today's famous Museum of Rajas', commonly known as Hason Raja Museum. It is situated at the heart (Zinda Bazar) of the Sylhet City Corporation area in Sylhet Division of Bangladesh. It is about 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) from the Sylhet Osmany International Airport and 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) from the Sylhet Railway Station. Maintained and organized by the Educationist Dewan Talibur Raja Trust, named after the grandson of Dewan Hason Raja. The museum's mission is to preserve and share the rich history of the great Raja Family of Sylhet keeping the Zamindar and Mystic poet Dewan Hason Raja Chowdhury (1854–1922) in the center, and the folk literature, folk music and mystic poets of Sylhet Division. The museum promotes a greater public awareness of the rich cultural legacy of Sylhet. In pursuit of these goals, this museum collects archival materials related to Bangla folk literature, music and poets from the greater Sylhet region, and preserves these collections in a repository, open to the public. The museum also encourages and facilitates research on folk literature and history. The results of this research are made available to the public through museum exhibits, publications and presentations. It was formally inaugurated on 30 June 2006 by thousands of folk loving people by playing "Ek Tara" (a folk musical instrument) together, which was a unique event of this kind.

review_text_clean: Nijhum Dwip নিঝুম দ্বীপ - Noakhali District Nijhum Dwip নিঝুম দ্বীপ which means Quiet Island, is a small island under Hatiya upazila. Total area of 14050 acres. It is situated in Noakhali District of Chittagong Division in Bangladesh. Once it was called Char Osman. A cluster of islands (mainly, Ballar Char, Kamlar char,Char Osman and Char Muri) emerged in the early 1950s as an alluvium in the shallow estuary of the Bay of Bengal On the south of Noakhali. These new sandbanks first drew the notice of a group of fishermen, who named it Baular Char (literally, the alluvium of sand) later transformed into Ballar Char. During winter, thousands of migratory birds flock in to island. The fishermen use the airy and sunny land as an ideal place for drying their catches from the sea. Sometimes many of them also construct straw huts on the island as seasonal residences. There are different types of animal at Nijhum Dwip. Spotted deer, Monkeys, Estuary reported to harbor the Ganges River Dolphin include Clawless Otter, Cat, Snakes, Tortoises and Turtles. During winter, thousands of migratory birds visit the islands and around a dozen of which are considered to be globally critically endangered, enhancing its splendor even further. In 1974 the Forest Department took a forestation program for a duration of twenty years in the north side of the island. Covering an area of nine thousand acres, it has now developed into a deep forest with a variety of plant species. Among the trees Keora is much seen. Besides this Gewa, Kankra, Bain, Babul, Karamja, Pashur and many other species are seen. On 8 th April, 2001 the government declared the 40390 acres of forest of Jahajmara range including 9550 acres of forest land on Nijhum Dwip as a National Park for the protection and development of the biodiversity of the forest. But in practice, there a very lazy appearance of that declaration. .How to Go: From Dhaka, Sadarghat toTamaruddin of Hatiya Dweep. Then Nijhum Dwip by local motor boat. Or Bus / Train to Chittagong. Then to Hatiya island by motor boat. From Hatiya to Jahazmara Bazar by tempo or jeep. Then to Amtali Ghat or Katakhali Ghat by rickshaw. These boats run depending on the wave and tide of sea.I loved the place! It's beautiful and adventurous at the same time. If you are travelling by road then be ready for some pain staking thrill while crossing Hatiya Island. Major part of the road is made of brick and damaged and you will have travel on a 'chander gari'. The sea truck crossing is also beautiful and 'mud-filled' at the same time (if they are not using the main dock). Travelling by the river using 'MV TASHRIF' is the most amazing part but time consuming as well! In this case there will be an additional 2:30 hrs journey by 'troller' is required which includes the non-stop breathtaking view of Monpura Island on the way. The place is nice and I really like to visit again!

review_text_clean: Nijhum Dwip Bangladesh: A Complete Travel Guide ￼ Nijhum Dwip is previously known as Char Osmani, Baluar Char, Golden Island, etc. which is located at Hatiya Upazila in Noakhali District Bangladesh. It is a little island occupying 164 Square kilometers, is a great tourist attraction in Bangladesh. It is surrounded by Bay of Bengal and Meghna River. Nijhum Dwip is a cluster of Islands. With the combination of Ballar Char, Kamlar Char, Char Osman and Char Muriform the Nijhum Island. Recently the government of Bangladesh declares this island as Nijhum Dwip National Park. Nijhum Dwip Location & Geographical Description It is mentioned earlier that Nijhum Dwip is encircled with the Bay of Bengal and Meghna Channel. It is two kilometers south-east from the Hatia upazilla and 120 kilometers south of Maijdee bazaar, Noakhali. Which According to the Google, Nijhum Dwip map Longitude and latitude are 21°35′0″N and 92°01′0″E respectively? This is 4-5 meter high from the sea level. History of Nijhum Island To find out the real history of this island we have talked with the local people living there. According to their information, More than 100 years ago, a fisherman of Bay of Bengal find this island but at that time, it was the primary stage which is under water. Time has been passed. Golden color sand forms this island. At that point, it was known as Golden Island. It was also known to all as Baluarchar. A Cowboy named Osman first build his house on this island. From that time, it was known as Char Osman. A Member of Parliament of Bangladesh changed this island’s name from Char Osman to Nijhum Dweep later. After 1970 people started to set up their houses on this island. How to go Nijhum Dwip from Dhaka From Dhaka Sadarghat regular steamer services are available to Hatia. MV Farhan, MV Tipu, etc. provide quite good services. It will cost 130 for standard deck rent to 1500. After reaching Tamruddin Ghat, there are two ways to reach Nijhum Island. You may choose a boat which approximate cost is about 2000 taka, or you may go by Baby Taxi which cost 400 takas. By baby taxis, you will reach Mortara Ghat. After crossing the river by boat which takes only 3-4 minute, you will reach Nijhum Dwip, your final destination. Weather of Nijhum Dwip The Climate of Nijhum Dwip almost remains the same around the year. The average Highest temperature of this island is around 32 degree Celsius, and the lowest is about 14 degree Celsius. During the rainy season, half of this island goes under water. People of Nijhum Dwip About 10000 people live there. Most of them are fishermen and some of them make their living by cultivating different kinds of agricultural product. There are six Bazaars which full filled the necessity of daily things and only the source of electricity. Two primary schools, 2 Madrasha, ten canals, 5.5 kilometers road and numerous ponds are available here. Nijhum Dwip Hotels Only one hotel named Hotel Abakash is available there which cost 500-2500 taka. You may choose to board. But they are not good at all. Recently there are some resorts are made near Nijhum Dwip. Nijhum Dwip travel guide If you don’t want to face a big wave of seas, it is the best time to visit from October to February. By this period, you can thoroughly enjoy the beauty of nature. If you don’t know how to swim, it will be the best practice to take lifejacket. Different Travel Agency offer different Nijhum Dwip tour packages. One can contact them and visit Nijhum Dwip easily.

review_text_clean: Shapla Beel, DBir Haor — Silent Poetry of Nature The Shapla Beel of DBir Haor in Sylhet is like a silent wonder of nature. During the monsoon season, this beel transforms into a vast water kingdom, and the combination of white and pink lotuses floating on its chest brings an unearthly beauty to the eyes. As far as the eye can see—only water, sky, and the fascination of lotuses. Riding a boat through the beel, it seems as if time slows down a little here. The light scent of kachuri leaves and lotuses in the air, the distant village houses, and the occasional call of birds—all combine to create a unique sense of peace. Away from the hustle and bustle of the city, Shapla Beel is an ideal place to get lost in the lap of nature. review_text_clean: DB Haor, Jaintapur, Sylhet. Last year, after seeing a picture of this place on a website, I had made a mental plan to try to come here this year. When I saw the picture, the Shapla season had just ended here. So there was no choice but to wait for a year. Of course, there is no shortage of Shapla in this country. However, for those who like to travel, there are two places in the country that are quite popular for seeing Shapla. One is in a village called Shatla in Ujirpur, Barisal, and the other is in Jaintapur, Sylhet. Shapla is available in Shatla during the monsoon and in Jaintapur during the winter. As winter approached, I had been planning to go to Jaintapur for a few days. At that time, I received an invitation to a batchmate-colleague's wedding in Sylhet. I did not want to be foolish enough to miss such an opportunity. Finally, after attending the wedding on December 15, I left for Jaintapur, 42 km from Sylhet, in the morning of December 16. There were 4 more people with me. After passing Jaintapur Bazar on the Sylhet-Tamabil road, a signboard appeared on the right hand side, which said DB Haor Special BGB Camp. After one km along that road, you will see DB Haor covered in millions of lotus flowers. The place is right on the Bangladesh-India border. Therefore, the hills of Meghalaya have increased the beauty of the place many times. This is where DB Haor sets itself apart from Shatla. The memory of Raja Ram Singh of Jainta state is intertwined with this DB Haor. He was drowned in this haor. In the middle of the haor stands a dilapidated temple, about 200 years old, with the memory of Raja Ram Singh. Lotus flowers remain in DB Haor for about 3/4 months. You can see this wonderful beauty only if you go in November-January. However, you have to go very early in the morning for this. When the sunlight falls on the lotus flowers, the petals of the flowers slowly close. It can be reached from Sylhet in an hour. We left Sylhet at 7 am and reached DB Haor around 8 am. If you go between 9.00-9.30 am, you will see the awake Shaplar. If they fall asleep, you will not be able to wake them up. You can go around the Haor by boat. If you go, you will definitely get on the boat. The fare will be 300 taka per hour. This fare is fixed by the upazila administration. 7/8 people can easily get on a medium-sized boat. How to go - Sylhet from any place in Bangladesh. From Sylhet, take a bus/laguna plying on the Sylhet-Tamabil route and get off at the board marked DB Haor a little after Jaintapur. The fare will be 40-50 taka per person. It takes about 1 hour. If you reserve CNG from Sylhet, the return fare will be around 1000 taka. We had reserved CNG. CNG is available for 1500 taka for the whole day. Please do not leave any kind of plastic items or do anything that spoils the beauty of nature while you are out and about.
review_text_original: ডিবির হাওর, জৈন্তাপুর, সিলেট। গতবছর একটা ওয়েবসাইটে এখানকার একটা ছবি দেখেই মনে মনে প্ল্যান করে রেখেছিলাম এবছর এখানে আসার চেষ্টা করবোই। যখন ছবিটা দেখি তখন মাত্র এখানে শাপলার সিজন শেষ হয়েছে। তাই একবছর অপেক্ষা করা ছাড়া উপায় ছিলোনা। এদেশে অবশ্য শাপলার বিলের অভাব নেই৷ তবে যারা ঘুরতে পছন্দ করেন তাদের কাছে দেশের মধ্যে শাপলা দেখার জন্য দুইটা জায়গা বেশ পছন্দের। একটা বরিশালের উজিরপুরের শাতলা নামক গ্রামে, আরেকটা সিলেটের জৈন্তাপুরে। শাতলায় শাপলা থাকে বর্ষায় আর জৈন্তাপুরে শীতে। শীত আসতেই জৈন্তাপুরে যাবো যাবো করছিলাম কিছুদিন ধরেই। ঠিক সেই সময়েই সিলেটে ব্যাচমেট-কলিগের বিয়ের দাওয়াত পেয়ে গেলাম। এমন সুযোগ হাতছাড়া করার বোকামি করতে চাইনি। শেষমেশ ডিসেম্বরের ১৫ তারিখ বিয়েতে এটেন্ড করে ১৬ই ডিসেম্বর একদম সকালেই রওনা দিলাম সিলেট থেকে ৪২ কি.মি. দূরের জৈন্তাপুরে। সাথে ছিলো আরো ৪ জন। সিলেট-তামাবিল সড়ক ধরে জৈন্তাপুর বাজার পেরিয়ে একটু এগোলেই হাতের ডানে একটা সাইনবোর্ড চোখে পড়ে যেখানে লেখা ডিবির হাওড় বিশেষ বিজিবি ক্যাম্প। সেই রাস্তা ধরে এক কি.মি. গেলেই চোখে পড়বে লাখ লাখ শাপলায় ছেয়ে থাকা ডিবির হাওর। জায়গাটা ঠিক বাংলাদেশ-ভারত সীমান্তে। তাই মেঘালয়ের পাহাড়গুলো যায়গাটার সৌন্দর্য্য বাড়িয়ে দিয়েছে বহুগুন। এখানেই ডিবির হাওর নিজেকে আলাদা করেছে শাতলার চেয়ে। জৈন্তা রাজ্যের রাজা রাম সিংহের স্মৃতি জড়িয়ে আছে এই ডিবির হাওরে। উনাকে এই হাওরে ডুবিয়ে মারা হয়েছিলো। হাওরের মাঝে দাঁড়িয়ে আছে রাজা রাম সিংহের স্মৃতি বিজড়িত প্রায় ২০০ বছরের পুরোনো জীর্ন একটি মন্দির। ডিবির হাওরে শাপলা থাকে মোটামুটি ৩/৪ মাস। নভেম্বর-জানুয়ারি গেলেই দেখা মিলবে এই অপরূপ সৌন্দর্য্যের। তবে এজন্য যেতে হবে একদম সকাল সকাল। সূর্যের আলো শাপলার গায়ে পড়লে আস্তে আস্তে ফুলগুলোর পাপড়ি বন্ধ হয়ে যায়। সিলেট থেকে এখানে পৌছানো যায় ঘন্টাখানেকের মধ্যেই। আমরা সিলেট থেকে সকাল ৭ টায় রওনা দিয়ে ৮ টার দিকে ডিবির হাওরে পৌছাই। মোটামুটি ৯.০০-৯.৩০ এর মধ্যে গেলে জাগ্রত শাপলার দেখা মিলবে। ওরা ঘুময়ে গেলে কিন্তু তখন আর ডেকে তুলতে পারবেন না। হাওরে নৌকায় ঘুরতে পারবেন। গেলে তো অবশ্যই নৌকায় উঠবেনই। ভাড়া নিবে ঘন্টায় ৩০০ টাকা। এই ভাড়া উপজেলা প্রশাসন থেকে নির্ধারন করে দেয়া। মাঝারি সাইজের এক নৌকায় ৭/৮ জন উঠা যায় অনায়াসেই। যেভাবে যাবেন- বাংলাদেশের যেকোন যায়গা থেকে সিলেট। সিলেট থেকে সিলেট-তামাবিল রুটে চলাচলকারী বাস/লেগুনায় করে জৈন্তাপুর এর একটু পরেই ডিবির হাওর লেখা ফলকের ওখানে নামবেন। ভাড়া নিবে জনপ্রতি ৪০-৫০ টাকা। সময় লাগে ১ ঘন্টার মত। সিলেট থেকে সিএনজি রিজার্ভ করে নিলে আসা-যাওয়া ভাড়া নিবে ১০০০ টাকার মত। আমরা সিএনজি রিজার্ভ করে গিয়েছিলাম। সারাদিনের জন্য সিএনজি ১৫০০ টাকায় পাওয়া যায়। দয়াকরে ঘুরতে গেলে সেখানে কোনপ্রকার প্লাস্টিক review_text_clean: DBir Haor located in Jaintapur, Sylhet is a beautiful tourist spot famous for thousands of red lotuses. Introduction to DBir Haor Location: According to Wikipedia information, it is located in Jaintapur Upazila of Sylhet, on the Bangladesh-India border and at the foot of the Meghalaya hills. Bills: DB, Yam, Horafkata and Kendri - these four bills form DBir Haor. Main attraction: After the monsoon, a lot of red lotuses grow naturally in this bill during winter or autumn. Best time to visit: Morning or early morning is the best time to see lotuses.

review_text_clean: DB Haor (commonly known as 'Lal Shaplar Beel') is a very picturesque wetland located at the foot of the Meghalaya Hills, bordering India, in Jaintapur Upazila of Sylhet District in northeastern Bangladesh. Every year at the beginning of winter, thousands of red lotuses bloom, turning the entire haor into a red carpet. ​Geographical location and structure ​DB Haor is mainly composed of four distinct beels: ​DB Beel ​Yam Beel ​Horfkata Beel ​Kendrikendri Beel ​The four beels together cover an area of ​​about 900 acres. The vast Khasia-Jaintia Hills of the Indian state of Meghalaya stand just behind the haor. ​Main attractions and beauty ​Red Lotus Fair: During autumn and winter (especially from October to January), countless red lotuses bloom throughout the entire water body. From a distance, it looks like a red sheet has been spread on the water. ​Reflection of Meghalaya Mountains: The reflection of the huge Meghalaya Mountains and clouds on the calm water creates a wonderful scene. ​Bird calls: A large number of native and migratory birds arrive here during the winter season, which is attractive for bird lovers. ​Historical background: According to local folklore and history, this area was once part of the Jainta kingdom. There are various monuments and old tombs associated with the memory of Jainta King Ramsingh next to the beel. ​Best time and schedule to visit ​Season: October to December/January is the best time to see the beauty of red lotus. ​Time of day: It is best to go between 6 am and 8 or 9 am. As the sun rises, the lotus flowers start to fade. ​Transportation ​From Sylhet city: From Kadamtali or Subhanighat in Sylhet city, take a bus or CNG-powered auto-rickshaw to Jaintapur Bazar (distance is about 40-42 km). ​From Jaintapur to Beel: You can easily reach DB Haor by tomtom, rickshaw or walking along the unpaved road past Jaintapur Bazar or Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) camp. ​Boat trip: Small indigenous boats are available for rent from local fishermen to explore the beel. ​Environmental protection precautions ​It is inappropriate to tear lotus flowers and leaves unnecessarily while traveling in a boat. ​It is important to refrain from throwing plastic or non-biodegradable waste to protect the environment and biodiversity of the haor. ​Since this is a border area, it is necessary to follow the instructions of the BGB and local administration.

আকর্ষণ ও সৌন্দর্য ​রক্তিম শাপলার মেলা: শরৎ ও শীতকালে (বিশেষ করে অক্টোবর থেকে জানুয়ারি) পুরো জলাশয় জুড়ে অগণিত লাল শাপলা ফোটে। দূর থেকে দেখলে মনে হয় যেন পানির ওপর লাল চাদর বিছিয়ে রাখা হয়েছে। ​মেঘালয় পাহাড়ের প্রতিফলন: শান্ত জলের বুকে বিশাল মেঘালয় পাহাড় ও মেঘের প্রতিচ্ছবি চমৎকার এক দৃশ্যের অবতারণা করে। ​পাখির কলকাকলি: শীতের মৌসুমে এখানে প্রচুর দেশি ও পরিযায়ী পাখির আগমন ঘটে, যা পাখিপ্রেমীদের জন্য আকর্ষণীয়। ​ঐতিহাসিক পটভূমি: স্থানীয় লোকগাথা ও ইতিহাস অনুযায়ী, এই এলাকা একসময় জৈন্তা রাজ্যের অংশ ছিল। বিলের পাশেই রয়েছে জৈন্তা রাজা রামসিংহের স্মৃতিবিজড়িত বিভিন্ন নিদর্শন ও পুরনো সমাধি। ​ভ্রমণের সেরা সময় ও সময়সূচি ​মৌসুম: অক্টোবর থেকে ডিসেম্বর/জানুয়ারি মাস লাল শাপলার সৌন্দর্য দেখার উপযুক্ত সময়। ​দিনের সময়: ভোর ৬টা থেকে সকাল ৮টা বা ৯টার মধ্যে যাওয়া সবচেয়ে ভালো। রোদ বাড়ার সাথে সাথে শাপলা ফুল বুজে যেতে শুরু করে। ​যাতায়াত ব্যবস্থা ​সিলেট শহর থেকে: সিলেট শহরের কদমতলী বা সুবহানীঘাট থেকে জাফলংগামী বাস বা সিএনজিচালিত অটোরিকশায় করে জৈন্তাপুর বাজারে পৌঁছাতে হয় (দূরত্ব প্রায় ৪০-৪২ কিমি)। ​জৈন্তাপুর থেকে বিল: জৈন্তাপুর বাজার বা বর্ডার গার্ড বাংলাদেশ (বিজিবি) ক্যাম্পের পাশ দিয়ে কাঁচা-পাকা রাস্তা দিয়ে টমটম, রিকশা বা হেঁটে সহজেই ডিবির হাওরে যাওয়া যায়। ​নৌকা ভ্রমণ: বিলের ভেতর ঘুরে দেখতে স্থানীয় মাঝিদের ছোট দেশি নৌকা ভাড়া পাওয়া যায়। ​পরিবেশ সুরক্ষায় সতর্কতা ​নৌকায় ঘোরার সময় অপ্রয়োজনে শাপলা ফুল ও পাতা ছেঁড়া অনুচিত। ​হাওরের পরিবেশ ও জীববৈচিত্র্য রক্ষায় প্লাস্টিক বা অপচনশীল বর্জ্য ফেলা থেকে বিরত থাকা জরুরি। ​এটি সীমান্তবর্তী এলাকা হওয়ায় বিজিবি ও স্থানীয় প্রশাসনের নির্দেশনা মেনে চলা আবশ্যক।

review_text_clean: Madhabkunda Waterfall is not just a tourist spot — it feels like nature suddenly decided to show off. The long walk through the green forest builds the excitement step by step, and then the sound of roaring water hits before the view does. When the waterfall finally appears, it’s powerful, misty, and honestly a little humbling. What I loved most is how the place changes your mood. The cool spray in the air, the echo of water crashing on rocks, and the surrounding hills make you forget phone notifications and city noise. If you stand quietly for a moment, you’ll hear birds, flowing streams, and wind through the trees — a full natural orchestra. The path is fairly easy but can be slippery near the waterfall, so good footwear helps. There are small shops outside for snacks and drinks, but the real refreshment is the cold natural air inside. Best time to visit is during or just after the rainy season when the waterfall is at its strongest and most dramatic. Great place for photos, but even better for just standing still and feeling small in front of something so powerful. A must-visit natural wonder of Bangladesh. I’d come again just to hear that sound of falling water.

review_text_clean: Madhabkunda Falls: Madhabkunda Falls is one of the highest waterfalls in Bangladesh. Located in Baralekha Upazila of Moulvibazar District, this waterfall is a popular tourist destination in Bangladesh. The surrounding forests, springs and ecological parks attract numerous tourists for picnics and day trips. Gangamara Falls flows 162 feet (49 m) down the rocky Patharia Hills to form the Madhabkunda Falls, which later merges with the Madhabchhara Falls below. The water of Madhabchhara flows westwards and finally meets the Hakaluki Haor. The main stream usually maintains a steady flow throughout the year. During the monsoon, a small river forms alongside the main river, and as the monsoon intensifies, the two rivers merge to form a powerful stream. This intense flow flows downstream and forms a huge pond below. As it falls into the pond, the depth of the pond continues to increase. The area is important to Hindus, with a temple nearby where Hindu rituals are held every year and a fair is held there. review_text_clean: The largest tea estate in Bangladesh is Finlay Tea Estate. Finlay Tea Estate is an important and ancient name in the history of the tea industry in Bangladesh. It began during the British colonial rule, in the late 19th century. The Scottish-based British business company James Finlay & Company established large-scale tea gardens in the Sylhet and Srimangal regions as part of the expansion of the tea industry in the subcontinent, within which Finlay Tea Estate was established. At that time, this region was very suitable for tea cultivation, so the British started producing tea here in a modern way. Finlay Tea Estate was mainly managed by the British and the tea here was exported to international markets including Europe. The development of worker settlements, railways and communication systems in the surrounding areas centered on this garden, which played a major role in shaping the economic structure of the entire Srimangal-Moulvibazar region. The colonial imprint is still visible in the plans of the manager bungalows, factory buildings and gardens built during the British period. After Bangladesh gained independence, many tea estates, including Finlay Tea Estate, underwent changes in ownership and management. Later, it was operated under local management and continues to make a significant contribution to the tea industry of Bangladesh. Today, Finlay Tea Estate is not only a production center, but also a tourist attraction for the natural beauty, historical environment and scenic views surrounding the tea estate. Overall, Finlay Tea Estate is a historical site deeply intertwined with the development of the tea industry in Bangladesh, British colonial history and the identity of the Srimangal region.

review_text_clean: Finlay Tea Estate is a traditional and ancient tea estate in Bangladesh, whose historical importance, natural beauty and economic contribution are all significant. It is mainly widely known in the Sylhet division - Srimangal and Moulvibazar regions. Finlay Tea's journey began during the British colonial period. It was founded by a Scottish company named James Finlay & Co., who developed the tea industry in various parts of India and Bangladesh. Even after Bangladesh became independent, the Finlay name remained and it is now operated as Finlay Tea Company (Bangladesh). They also have many lands and tea factories in Srimangal and Moulvibazar. Finlay Tea Estates produce high-quality orthodox and CTC tea. The estates have their own processing units (tea factories) where full-bodied tea is prepared from green tea leaves. Some estates also produce rubber and timber. Finlay Tea is known in the export market in addition to the domestic market in Bangladesh. The company is one of the oldest and largest tea companies in the country, with a well-organized tea garden, tea processing center, and marketing system.

It is a unique natural treasure, formed by a combination of rivers, canals, and low-lying lands that create a vast water-based ecosystem. In 2000, Tanguar Haor was declared a Ramsar Site, which means it is recognized internationally as a wetland of great ecological importance. It became the second Ramsar Site in Bangladesh after the Sundarbans. The haor covers a huge area and contains more than forty smaller wetlands, known locally as "beels." During the rainy season, Tanguar Haor turns into a massive sheet of water, almost like a sea, connecting with the sky at the horizon. In winter, the water level decreases, revealing wide stretches of grassland and creating a completely different landscape. This seasonal change makes the haor look different throughout the year. The haor is home to rich biodiversity. Every winter, thousands of migratory birds travel from Siberia and the Himalayan region to take shelter here. Various species of fish, aquatic plants, and freshwater turtles also live in this wetland, making it an important habitat for wildlife. Tanguar Haor has also become a popular tourist destination, especially between November and February. Visitors enjoy boat rides across the vast water, bird watching, and the beautiful view of the Meghalaya hills in the background. Nearby places like Neeladri Lake and Tekerghat add extra charm to the journey. However, the haor faces serious threats due to illegal fishing, encroachment, and excessive tourism. Local authorities and environmentalists are working to protect its natural balance so that future generations can also enjoy this treasure. In conclusion, Tanguar Haor is not only a beautiful natural site but also an important part of Bangladesh's ecological wealth. Protecting it should be a shared responsibility of the government, local people, and visitors alike.

review_text_clean: Tanguar Haor – A Hidden Paradise in Bangladesh ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Tanguar Haor, located in Sunamganj district, is one of Bangladesh's most breathtaking wetlands, covering around 100 square kilometers. This vast haor (floodplain) is surrounded by the Meghalaya hills of India and consists of over 50 small villages, making it a unique blend of water, land, and rural life. Natural Beauty & Experience During the monsoon season, Tanguar Haor turns into a vast, serene lake where boats become the only mode of transport. The endless blue waters, the reflection of the sky, and the distant green hills create a mesmerizing view. In winter, it becomes home to thousands of migratory birds, making it a paradise for bird watchers and photographers. Best Time to Visit Monsoon (June–September): For the best boating experience and breathtaking views. Winter (November–February): Ideal for bird watching and enjoying the calm waters. Things to Do Boat rides – Experience the vastness of the haor on a traditional wooden boat. Camping – Stay overnight on a boat or in nearby villages to enjoy the peaceful surroundings. Exploring Barek Tila – A nearby hilltop offering a spectacular view of Tanguar Haor. Why Visit? Tanguar Haor is not just a tourist destination—it is a Ramsar wetland, recognized for its ecological significance. It offers a rare combination of natural beauty, biodiversity, and local culture, making it a must-visit for nature lovers, adventure seekers, and photographers.

review_text_clean: Tanguar haor is unique wetland ecosystem with enormous natural beauty. This haor having an area of 100sq km and consisting of 120 small and large (canals) is in its youth during the monsoon. During the winter the haor becomes home migratory birds. Nature lovers and tourists may make an arrangement for at least two days to make a trip to the fascinating Tanguarhaor. Tanguarhaor is located in the Dharmapasha and Tahirpur upazilas of Sunamganj District Bangladesh covering 10 villages. This wetland is home to about 208 species of birds, 150 species of water plants, 34 species of reptiles and 11 species of amphibious. There are more than 140 species of fresh water fish in the haor. You can have a taste of the haor fishes if you make a visit to the haor. The more predominant among them are: rui, katol, ayir, boal, gang magur, tara, baim, gulsha, gutum, tengra, titna, gaajar, garia, beti, kakia etc. Leuchchhamara and Berberiabils are free abodes for birds of many species in Tanguarhaor. Besides, you will find birds in other bils, including RouarBil, GazariarBil, AlomerDoar, SangsarBil, KoikhaliBil, ChhunkholaBil, JittolarGop, FoillarBil, RupabhuiBil, Sattar Bil, MoisherGata, BaloarDoba, AmchharerBil, KauarBil, AnsarerBil, KhajuriBil, AinnarBil and NolkathirBil. Keeping a binocular while travelling will make watching the birds more enjoyable. You can choose either of Shyamoly Paribahan, Hanif Enterprize, Ena Paribaha and Mamun Paribahan, if you want to go to Sunamganj from Dhaka by road. The bus tickets will be available within the range of 55o taka. You have to get off at Surma Bridge before entering Sunamganj town. From there, you have to go to Tahirpur or Solemanpur by leguna or bike. However, it is better to go to solemanpur in February because water level in Boulai (Tahirpur to Solemanpur) falls during this period. You will have to pay 800 to 1200 taka to hire a leguna to reach Solemanpur from Sunamganj. At least 8 people can get on board of a leguna. A motorbike will charge 300 to 400 taka for two persons. From Solemanpur you have to hire engine-driven boat to reach Tanguarhaor through Patlai River. You have to pay 1000 to 1500 taka each day to hire an engine-run boat. You can even stay on these boats at night. You have to buy cooking ingredients to take with you while visiting. You will need to take necessary medicines, camera and back-up charger for mobile phone. You can stay at Tahirpur Dakbanglow if you wish to.

review_text_clean: I visited Hum Hum Waterfall in June, and it turned out to be one of the most challenging yet rewarding trips I’ve taken. The trail was muddy, slippery, and demanded a lot of effort — but the waterfall was at its fullest and most powerful, making every step worthwhile. Hum Hum sits deep inside the Rajkandi Reserve Forest in Moulvibazar. From Sreemangal, we traveled to Kolabonpara village, where our local guide was waiting. I can’t stress this enough — a guide is essential. The trails are unmarked, and in the rainy season, the forest can change quickly, with new muddy sections, stream crossings, and hidden hazards. The trek took about two and a half hours each way. From the very start, the path tested us. The recent rains had turned parts of the trail into slippery clay, and some sections were steep enough that we had to hold on to bamboo or tree roots for balance. Several stream crossings required careful footwork, with wet rocks ready to trip you if you rushed. Despite the difficulty, the forest was alive and beautiful. Towering bamboo groves and thick undergrowth surrounded us. Birds called from somewhere high above, and every now and then we’d hear the rustle of wildlife in the distance. The air smelled fresh and earthy, the kind of scent you only find deep in the forest after rain. The sound of the waterfall reached us before the sight did — a deep, constant roar that grew louder with each turn. By the time we stepped into the clearing, all the exhaustion disappeared. Hum Hum in June is breathtaking. A tall cascade of white water thundered down the moss-covered cliff, sending a mist into the air that cooled us instantly. The pool at the base shimmered under the sunlight, and the force of the falling water created a constant spray. Standing there, you could feel the raw power of nature all around you. We rested on the boulders near the pool, dipping our feet into the cold water. A couple of people from our group braved the slippery rocks and got closer, getting completely soaked — but smiling the whole time. There are no benches, or built-up structures here. It’s just you, the water, and the forest, exactly how it should be. The trek back was quicker but still tricky. Slippery downhill slopes in wet conditions require even more care, and by the time we reached the village, our shoes were heavy and our legs were sore. But we were all smiling — because Hum Hum had delivered on every promise. Tips from My Visit in June: 1.Wear strong hiking shoes with good grip — this is not a sandal-friendly trail. 2.Bring plenty of drinking water and some snacks. 3.Be prepared for mud and slippery ground — pace yourself and use a walking stick if possible. 4.Hire a local guide — they know the safe routes and stream crossings. ★Respect the environment — carry your trash back. ★★★Final Thoughts: Hum Hum in June is not an easy trip. The trek is long, muddy, and slippery, and it will test your stamina and balance. But when you finally stand in front of that roaring waterfall, surrounded by lush green forest, you’ll know it was worth every step. This is nature at its rawest and most beautiful, and one of the most rewarding adventures you can have in Bangladesh.

review_text_clean: Together me and my wife we went for a day long trekking to Hum Hum Waterfalls during the end of this July from Sreemangal..! Located in Moulvibazar district, this is very close to the Indian border, you have to go to Sreemangal from Dhaka by bus, train or private vehicle. And, there is no proper place for families at, or, around the Hum Hum Waterfalls for night stay. So, it must be a day trip to and from this place. Though, few of my traveler and Cyclist friends took tents with them and camped during the night just outside of the forest. This was a great journey this time to the falls, some places the path was muddy, some slippery, some places you had to cross small strings, galleys and canals..! You will have to climb up and down walking both the ways.. through a jungle trail. During rainy season, there would be leeches found on your feet few times, not big deal at all, however check often. Its an excellent trail to trek, so this is not at all only about the Water Falls..! A must to go place..!!! As said earlier, in most/ usual cases it has to be a day trip. So, start from Sreemangal by 7:00/ 7:30 am, DO NOT START LATE...!!! How to go to and from Sreemangal from Dhaka: i) By bus: Hanif Poribahan (bus service) and Shyamoli Poribahan have bus to Sreemangal every hour all day long..! Ena has AC buses on in the morning and another in the afternoon (google for latest update). However, if would like to save hotel bills you may travel both ways during the nights. Bus starts from Sayedabad, each of the bus companies have their ticket counters for purchasing the ticket and waiting. For AC Bus: it might take something like 700 or 800 taka one way, for non AC 450 taka..! Caution: If you have a weak heart please do not dare to go by Hanif, they drive like Nascar drivers..! ii) By Train: All the train from Dhaka starts from Komlapur Rail Station, there is a train that starts in the morning and another at 9:30 pm in the evening. Train fare starts from 240 to 1,000 taka. However, the night train reaches Sreemangal as early as 2:30 am/ 3:00 am/ 3:30 am that is inconvenient for many reasons, accordingly choose day time train if you are wiling and enthusiast about train. iii) By Cycle or private/ hired car: Its only 180 Km road trip from Dhaka, so no matter what you take its great journey. You may follow Dhaka to Sylhet Highway through Kulshi 300 feet road, Kanchanpur bridge, Maona, Sylhet highway..! Quality of Road is fine all the ways only need to be a bit more careful during Kanchanpur to Maona and Voirob to Bramhanbaria junction due to more traffic in these sections. Transport: From Sreemangal you may take CNG Auto Rickshaw for the whole day to go and come back with the same one. The Auto Rickshaw will wait for the whole day until you come back. You wont get anything from there on the way back, if you don't contract for the whole day. It will take 1,500 to 2,000 taka for the whole day. Nothing additional. You may take a Chander Gari (old 4 wheel jeep) it would go further than CNG upto Kolabon para.. and would be faster with 3,000 to 4,000 taka for the whole day. From Kolabon para.. it is around 4 Km trekking/ hiking..! Food and Drinks: Take dry food and energy/ peanut/ chocolate bar, dry dates, water, Chanachur, chips/ fries.. with you..! As there wont be any shop both ways. You would get bottled water, packet snacks at the falls site. But be very care not litter but bring with foils and packs with you for the sake of environment. Trekking Guide: At the entry gate of you would get some tea garden laborer and locals sitting, you would get a guide within 400 taka.. for the entire day.. till the end of the trip. Guides are good and reliable..! We had Bidhan as guide, you may also search for him. Caution: Start as early as possible in the morning, don’t litter, prefer a Chander Gari (old jeep), take some dry food and water with you. Have a Great Trip...!!!

review_text_clean: About Uncover the hidden beauty of Humhum water Falls. Who dare to discover true wild life and see mighty Hamham by himself...? Description Hammam Waterfall, Bangladesh - Humhum is the name of a waterfall. This is located at Kamalganja, Moulvibazar district of Bangladesh. People of that location pronounces this as Humhum, in some Print media it is also written as Humhum. But the real spelling would be Hammam. I got this confirmation from some local educated people, who includes govt officials and school teachers. We were four in our team and i was the youngest. By the by, I am running now 42 years and rest all are 47-48 years old. Quite young and energetic a team, no doubt. On 13 February,2011, we went to Kamalganja bazaar. This bazaar is about 20 minutes ride from Srimangal. After reaching there, we were in a dilemma about passing the night. However, lastly we got two rooms in a local boarding house and somehow passed the night by gossiping. On 14 February, 2011; at 07 a m we started from this bazaar and reached Karma BOP after 30 minutes drive. From this location our foot march started. I will narrate the details of the journey in the following paragraphs. The main beauty of this waterfall is in it's surrounding ground features. Anybody visiting this place will enjoy the whole route to the fall. But the final climax of the beauty is in the waterfall itself. Location This waterfall is located at Kamalganja Upazilla of MaulviBazar district of Bangladesh. Karma BOP is the last vehicle pliable point. The tea garden of National Tea Company is located beside this BOP. From the BOP, we moved by 3 motorcycles to the last edge of tea garden, which is about 5 km. From this point, we started our route march to reach the waterfall. You want to go there? OK, I am describing you. The Road to Hammam The total walking time is about 2 hours 30 minutes to reach the destination. If you plan to move to see the waterfall, following precautionary arrangements should be made: 1. Be mentally ready to walk on bare foot. 2. Carry a small pack with you for carrying a camera, If possible a GPS, a water bottle and light first aid items. 3. Don't forget to get a guide from the Karma Bazar to lead you. 4. Have a bamboo stick while walking to avoid slips and fall. The whole route is full of numerous types of landscapes. From the very start point you will be walking through a forest with some some small hillocks. After walking through this for about 30 minutes, you will have to get down in a natural fountain (locally called chhara or nala), where you will have to walk trough water. The height of this water level will vary from ankle level to your thigh level time to time. You may find some people cutting bamboo in and around that fountain. Even if you don't meet them end route, you will come across the signs of bamboo extraction in that fountain. Be very careful while walking through those as to avoid leg injury by those. In many places, You will find the bottom surface of the fountain is with stones. At times those are very slippery. You need to be more careful while walking through those. That is why i mentioned for a stick to use as a support.

review_text_clean: The Heart of Rajshahi’s Riverfront! ​As a frequent traveler and Local Guide, I can confidently say that the T-Groin (locally known as T-Badh) is the soul of Rajshahi city. This T-shaped hydraulic structure, originally built to protect the city from the Padma’s erosion, has evolved into the most popular social hub for locals and tourists alike. ​The Experience & Popularity: The atmosphere here is electric, especially during late afternoons. It’s the perfect spot to catch a breeze and watch the sunset over the horizon. During the monsoon, the water level rises right up to the concrete blocks, creating a sea-like vibe, while in the winter, the vast "Char" (river islands) emerge, offering a different kind of beauty. It is almost always crowded on weekends, reflecting its status as the city's top hangout spot. ​Boat Rides & The Sandbars (Char): One of the highlights of visiting T-Badh is taking a traditional engine boat or a speed boat across the Padma. For a small fee (usually BDT 50-100 per person for group trips), you can reach the massive sandbars in the middle of the river. These "chars" feel like a mini-desert where you can walk for miles. It’s a must-do for photographers and nature lovers. ​Food & Street Delicacies: The food scene here is vibrant and affordable. The area is famous for: ​Fuchka & Chotpoti: Numerous stalls offer some of the best spicy snacks in the city. ​Street Snacks: Kalai Ruti (a local Rajshahi specialty made of black gram flour) is often available nearby and is a must-try with duck meat or eggplant mash. ​Tea: Numerous tea stalls line the embankment, perfect for "adda" (socializing). ​Pro-Tips for Visitors: ​Timing: Visit between 4:00 PM and 6:30 PM to witness the breathtaking sunset. ​Safety: If you take a boat ride, ensure the boat isn't overloaded, especially during the monsoon when the current is strong. ​Cleanliness: As a Local Guide, I urge everyone to keep this beautiful embankment clean by using the designated bins for plastic waste. ​Whether you are a local student or a traveler visiting from afar, your trip to Rajshahi is incomplete without a walk along the T-Badh.

review_text_clean: A Serene Escape by the Padma River Rajshahi's T-Badh, aptly named for its distinctive "T" shape, is far more than just a protective embankment against the mighty Padma River's erosion. It has evolved into a beloved recreational hub and a symbol of the city's connection to its majestic river. This scenic spot offers a tranquil escape from the urban bustle, drawing both locals and tourists with its picturesque views and calming ambiance. The primary draw of T-Badh is the breathtaking panorama of the Padma River, especially at sunset. As the sun dips below the horizon, it paints the sky in vibrant hues, which are beautifully reflected on the river's calm waters, creating a truly mesmerizing spectacle. The gentle breeze, the rhythmic lapping of the waves, and the vast open sky combine to create a deeply soothing experience. Visitors often take leisurely strolls along the embankment, enjoying the fresh air and the natural beauty. Beyond its scenic appeal, T-Badh offers a lively atmosphere, particularly in the afternoons and evenings. You'll find numerous food stalls offering local snacks and refreshments, adding to the vibrant community feel. Boat rides on the Padma are a popular activity, providing a unique perspective of the river and its surroundings. While primarily a place for relaxation and enjoyment of nature, T-Badh also serves as a testament to the ongoing efforts to protect Rajshahi from the river's powerful currents, showcasing a blend of functionality and natural charm. It's an essential stop for anyone visiting Rajshahi, offering a true taste of its riverside charm.

review_text_clean: Varendra Research Museum: Varendra Museum is a museum located in the heart of Rajshahi city, Bangladesh, which serves as a major research center and tourist attraction. It houses over 19,000 historical artifacts from the Indian subcontinent, especially the Varendra region of northern Bangladesh. It is run by the University of Rajshahi. It is considered the oldest museum in Bangladesh, as it was the first museum established in East Bengal on 27 September 1910. The museum began its journey as the collection of the Varendra Research Association and received its present name in 1919. The kings of Rajshahi and Natore, especially Prince Sarat Kumar Roy, donated their personal collections to the Varendra Museum. Varendra refers to an ancient city. Varendra (or Barinda) was a region of Bengal, which is now in Bangladesh. It included the Pundravardhan or Pundra kingdom. According to Cunningham, Varendra was bounded on the west by the Ganges and Mahananda, on the east by the Karatoya, on the south by the Padma, and on the north by the Cooch Behar and the Terai. The Varendra Brahmins originated from this region. The Varendra settlement, known as Janakbhavu (fatherland), was one of the most prosperous regions of the ancient Indian subcontinent. Literary and epigraphic evidence shows that a distinct artistic community had attained wide fame here during the Pala dynasty, and this artistic tradition continued uninterruptedly until the Sena dynasty. Main Collections and Galleries: The museum houses about 19,000 artifacts spanning several millennia, including artifacts from the Indus Valley, Pala, Sena, Maurya and Gupta periods. The museum's collection is spread across seven galleries, showcasing thousands of years of civilization: • Gallery 1: This houses the collection of the Indus Valley Civilization (2500 BCE) and some of the 265 artifacts recovered from the excavations at Sompur Paharpur (8th-12th centuries). It also houses ancient Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian inscriptions. There is also a significant collection of gold and silver coins from various economic and political periods. • Galleries 2-5: This houses rare stone, bronze and modern wooden sculptures of Buddhist, Hindu (Surya, Shiva, Vishnu, Durga and various Bodhisattvas from the Pala, Sena, Maurya and Gupta periods) and Jain gods and goddesses. • Gallery 6: This displays Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and ancient Bengali inscriptions and carved stones from the Muslim period. Handwritten Holy Quran, Arabic and Persian inscriptions and Sher Shah's bronze cannon are displayed here. There are more than 10,000 books and 15,000 rare manuscripts in Sanskrit, Bengali and Arabic. • A new gallery has been added to showcase the indigenous and tribal culture of the Rajshahi region. The traditional culture, tools and jewellery of the indigenous people of the Rajshahi region are displayed here. Opening hours: Saturday – Wednesday: 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM. Friday: 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM (with a prayer break from 1:00 PM to 2:30 PM). Thursday: Closed for weekends.

review_text_clean: The Barind Research Museum is located at Hetem Khan, the heart of the Rajshahi metropolis. This is the first museum in Bangladesh. It is one of the archeological collections in South Asia. Sarat Kumar Roy, zamindar of the Dighapatiya royal family of Natore, lawyer Akshay Kumar Maitreya and teacher of Rajshahi Collegiate School Ramprasad Chandra have made significant contributions to the establishment of the Barind Museum. In 1910, they formed the Barindra Research Society to collect and preserve the heritage and artifacts of Bengal. In that year, they searched various places in Rajshahi and collected 32 rare specimens. Construction of the museum's own building began on land donated by Sarat Kumar Roy to preserve the artefacts. Construction was completed in 1913 AD. The museum was inaugurated on 13 November of the same year by the then Governor of Bengal, Carmichael. The foundation stone of Lord Carmichael was laid in 1911. The Calcutta Museum suddenly demanded all the artefacts preserved in it. At the initiative of the then Governor Carmichael, the Barind Museum was given the authority to collect and preserve its artefacts through an official notification issued on 14 February 1913. In 1923, Calcutta University jointly with the museum authorities began excavations at the Paharpur Buddhist Monastery in Naogaon. Later, 258 specimens were discovered from Paharpur in a single effort of the Barind Research Society. After 1947, there was a crisis over the existence of the museum. From 1949 to 1961, half of the museum building was used as a medical school. When the museum was about to close in 1984, Rajshahi University acquired its movable and immovable property on October 10 of that year. Among the visitors of the museum are Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose and many other famous personalities.

review_text_clean: The Varendra Research Museum, established in 1910 by the Varendra Investigation Society, is not only the oldest museum in Bangladesh but also the first museum to be established in erstwhile East Bengal.It got its current name in 1919.It stands as a contribution of some of the enlightened citizens like Kumar Sarat Kumar Ray of Dighapatia, Akshaya Kumar Maitreya, and Ramaprasad Chanda.The museum's collection contains eleven different galleries exhibiting various antique religious sculptures and archaeological finds.There are collections from the Indus Valley Civilization and 265 items from Sompur.Various domestic wares made of metal,alloys,terracotta and ceramic are exhibited there.There are archaeological relics from the Muslim period.Most of the galleries display the sculptures of Hindu and Buddhist gods and goddesses.Notable Hindu gods and goddesses are Brahma,Vishnu,Siva,Surya,Ganapati,Bhairava,Parvati,Uma,Kali,Ganga,Chamund,Manasa,Sarwashwati,Varah,Vaishnabi etc.Buddhist relics include the sculptures of Yamari,Buddha,Manjusri,Manjuvara etc.There are some galleries exhibiting Arabic,Persian,Sanskrit and old Bengali stone inscriptions.There is a collection of old coins and documents.There is a Mihrab representing the Muslim heritage.The pictures of Muslim emperors such as Bahadur Shah,Aurangzeb,Shahjahan,Jahangir,Akbar,Humayun,Babur and Muhammad Shah are displayed in a particular gallery.The war weapons of different times,masks,folk music instruments and dresses of renowned persons of the royal families are shown in a gallery.From 1964 until now the museum has remained a part of Rajshahi University.

review_text_clean: I Badh (or "I Bandh") is not a typical scenic ghat. It is an embankment—a long, rugged, earthen wall built to hold back the colossal might of the Padma River. Visiting here is less about tranquil sunsets and more about witnessing a stark, powerful dialogue between human endeavor and relentless nature. The scenery is dramatic, humbling, and deeply atmospheric. The Scenic Character: The view is dominated by the embankment itself, a raised roadway that acts as your stage. From this vantage point, you look down onto the vast, sandy chars and the distant river channel on one side, and over the protected, lower-lying land on the other. This unique perspective frames the landscape like a living map. · The Monumental Scale: The true spectacle is the sheer expanse. During the dry season, the Padma retreats, revealing miles of golden, sculpted sandbanks (chars) that stretch towards the hazy horizon. The river itself becomes a shimmering silver thread in the distance. It’s a panorama of breathtaking, almost desert-like emptiness, conveying the scale of the force this badh must contain. · The Seasonal Drama: This is where the scenery tells its most potent story. · In the Dry Winter: The landscape is serene, almost melancholic. Local life spreads onto the chars for farming, fishing, and grazing. The air is clear, perfect for long, contemplative walks along the bund, watching kite flyers against the vast blue sky. · In the Raging Monsoon: The mood transforms entirely. The Padma rises, angry and powerful, its turbulent, muddy waters beating against the very foot of the badh. The once-distant river is now a roaring, intimidating presence. Standing on the embankment, feeling the spray and wind, you viscerally understand its purpose—it is a frontline against the flood, a silent guardian. · Life on the Line: The scenery is animated by the resilient communities that live in its shadow. You'll see fishermen launching boats from the sandy shores, farmers tending to crops on the chars, and children playing on slopes that become a barrier for survival in a few months. This human element adds a poignant, resilient layer to the vast natural canvas. Ambiance: The atmosphere is one of solitude and raw power. It’s often quiet, save for the constant wind that sweeps across the open space. There’s a tangible sense of exposure to the elements—sun, wind, and the latent force of the river. It’s a place for introspection, for feeling small yet connected to a grand, cyclical struggle. Verdict: I Badh offers a fundamentally different, more raw scenic experience than the typical riverfront. It is not conventionally pretty; it is impressive and sobering. It provides a profound lesson in geography, human resilience, and the untamed personality of the Padma. Come here not for leisure, but for perspective. Come to stand on the rampart, feel the wind, and watch a landscape that breathes with the seasons, all held in a tense, beautiful balance by the earth beneath your feet. Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5) for its unique, powerful, and authentic landscape. A must-see for those interested in the true, unvarnished relationship between land, water, and life in riverine Bangladesh.

review_text_clean: Shaheed A.H.M Qamaruzzaman Central Park and Zoo: Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park and Zoo is a large public park and zoo located in Rajshahi, Bangladesh. Spread over 33 acres on the banks of the beautiful Padma River, this park serves as one of the city's most popular recreational centers for students and tourists, combining natural beauty, diverse species of wildlife, and modern entertainment facilities. The park is named after A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman, a prominent national leader and one of the four prominent figures martyred in 1975. During the British colonial period, the area where the park is now located, near the bend of the Padma River, was used as a horse racing ground. After the British left, the land remained abandoned for many years, until in the early 1970s, local political leader Abul Hasnat Muhammad Kamaruzzaman took the initiative to turn this abandoned site into a public park under the Rajshahi Zilla Parishad. The park was officially inaugurated in 1972, later a zoo was added inside the park in 1983, and in 1996, the Rajshahi City Corporation took over its management. The park has a variety of attractions for visitors of all ages. The zoo section houses a variety of wildlife including Bengal tigers, chital deer, crocodiles, monkeys, pythons and numerous species of birds such as peacocks and pelicans, A central lake offers paddle boat rides, A small lake shelters fish and aquatic birds, creating a peaceful natural habitat, A children's play area with a seesaw, swings and slides. The park is known for its lush greenery, which includes walking paths surrounded by eucalyptus and fruit trees and various artistic sculptures, a butterfly garden and an artificial hill and a beautifully designed bridge from which a picturesque view of the Padma River can be seen. There are also shaded picnic areas, an amphitheater and designated parking facilities near the main entrance. Operating Hours: 8:00 AM – 6:00 PM daily.

review_text_clean: The Puthia Rajbari, also known as the Five-Anna Zamindar House, was the residence of Maharani Hemantakumari Devi. Among the archaeological heritage sites of Bengal, Puthia Rajbari in Rajshahi is one of the most notable. In 1895, Maharani Hemantakumari Devi constructed the present rectangular two-storied palace in an attractive Indo-European architectural style. It is located about 32 km northeast of the Rajshahi district সদর, along the Natore highway beside the Bagha–Puthia district road. One can reach Puthia by bus from any part of the country, and also easily by road after getting down at Natore or Rajshahi via train. In the 17th century, during the Mughal period, the Puthia zamindari was one of the oldest estates in Bengal. It is said that a man named Nilambar received the title of “Raja” from the Mughal emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605–1627), after which it became known as Puthia Rajbari. In 1744, the estate was divided—where the eldest son received five and a half annas of the property, and the other three sons received three and a half annas collectively. The zamindari system continued until 1950, when it was abolished, along with the Puthia estate. However, despite the abolition, the palaces, temples, and other structures built during that era still stand today. This palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemantakumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law, Maharani Sarat Sundari Devi. The front portion of the building features beautifully crafted pillars, decorations, wooden works, and floral and vine motifs on the walls and above the doors, showcasing exquisite architectural artistry. The roof of the palace is flat, constructed with iron beams, wooden supports, and tiles. A moat was dug around the palace for security purposes. There are six large royal ponds surrounding Puthia Rajbari, each covering about six acres. There are also six temples nearby, the largest being the Shiva Temple (Puthia). Other temples include the Radha Gobinda Temple, Gopal Temple, Govinda Temple, and Dol Mancha. Each temple is adorned with exquisite terracotta artwork on its walls. The complex also includes Jor-Bangla temples, bungalow-style temples, and Pancharatna (five-spired) temples—each representing different architectural styles of Bengal. Additionally, there are the queen’s bathing ghat and the inner quarters, making the entire palace complex vast and impressive. Puthia Rajbari is surrounded on all sides by moats. These were either built to prevent enemy intrusion or created while raising the land, as the area was previously low-lying. 04 April, 26

The palace is located 30 km east of the city on the Rajshahi-Natore highway and one km south of the Rajshahi-Natore highway in Puthia upazila. It is famous for its Indo-Saracenic revival architecture and the historic Hindu temple complex that surrounds it. It was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in memory of her mother-in-law Maharani Saratsundari Devi. review_text_clean: Initially, Puthia was a village of Laskarpur Pargana, named after Laskar Khan Nilamber, the brother of the first zamindar of Puthia, who was the first to receive the title of Raja from the Mughal emperor Jahangir. A partition of the estate took place in 1744 and the zamindari was divided among 4 co shares among whom the panch ani (five annas) and char ani (four annas) co-shares become famous in conducting jamindary. Puthia Rajbari is surrounded by ditches. The south end of an open field is where panch ani palace is situated. 4.31 acres of land was used for the Rajbari. The once strong walls surrounding the place are now damaged in places. The rajbari is divided into 4 courts : Kachhari (office) Angan (court) Mandir angan or Gobindabari (temple court) Andar Mahal (inner quarters) Residence of Maharani Hemanti Kumari The rooms are built around the courts in the palace, with the exception of the Kachari Angan, the courts are one storeyed. Kachari Angan has porticos on both the west and east ends which project in the Palladian manner. The west entrance gate leads to Kachari Angan while the other leads to Temple or Gobindabari courts. Each portico is supported by 4 semi-Corinthian columns rising the full height of the building. The porticos contain arcaded, semi-glazed loggias at the first floor level. The building's central portion, between the porticos, continues the columned theme and also has a loggia at first floor level. Also here the 4 semi Corinthian pillars cover the upper parts of the building. A wooden staircase leads to the upper floor on the east side. There are three rooms of different size, two of which were used as treasuries. The other side, (Western) has 4 rooms with two verandahs. Close to Govindabari, there are two small rooms with verandah. Now, most of the rooms built on the east and south of Kachari Angan are at ruins. The northern block of the building with east–west axis is double storeyed and has a wide hall of 21.95m x 7.16m. The upper storeyed portion has six variously announced rooms. In front of the hall there is a wide verandah with balconies on either side. The Pancharatna Bara Gobinda temple is located at the Gobindabari of this palace. The temple is beautifully ornamented with terracotta carvings. There are two rooms and several bathrooms in the western part of Andar Mahal. Most of the rooms in the court in western part of Andar Mahal are in ruins. In the eastern part of Ander Mahal there is one storeyed residence of Rani Hemanta Kumari. It has a porch in front of it and a central reception hall with nine rooms. There are extended verandahs with arches in front and rear of the hall room. Iron and wooden beams have been used in the roof.

review_text_clean: During the seventeenth century, in the Mughal era, the Puthia Zamindari was one of the oldest among the various kingdoms of Bengal at that time. It is said that a man named Nilambar received the title of "Raja" from the Mughal Emperor Jahangir (1605–1627 AD), after which the estate became known as the Puthia Rajbari (Royal Palace). In 1744, the zamindari was divided — the eldest son of the zamindar received five and a half annas of the property, while the other three sons received three and a half annas. The zamindari system continued until 1950. When the system was abolished, the Puthia zamindari also came to an end. However, even though the zamindari system was abolished, the palace, temples, and other structures built during that era still remain intact. review_text_clean: Puthia Rajbari is not just a palace; it is the centerpiece of the most impressive collection of historic Hindu temples in Bangladesh. Located about 30 km east of Rajshahi city, this site is a masterclass in Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture and a must-visit for history buffs and photography enthusiasts. 🏛️ The Experience: What to Expect Walking into the Puthia complex feels like stepping back into the late 19th century. The main palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law. 1. The Royal Palace (Rajbari) The palace itself is a grand, two-story structure with a symmetrical facade and massive Corinthian columns. * The Vibe: It’s a mix of colonial elegance and local decay. While the front facade is relatively well-maintained and houses a small museum, the back portions are in various states of ruin, which adds a haunting, "forgotten kingdom" atmosphere. * Must-See: Look for the intricate floral plaster reliefs and the multicolored glass still clinging to some of the windows. 2. The Temple Complex (The Real Star) The Rajbari is surrounded by several temples that are often more architecturally significant than the palace itself: * Bhubaneshwar Shiva Temple: The largest Shiva temple in the country. Its five soaring spires (Pancha Ratna) and the massive black basalt Shiva Lingam inside are breathtaking. * Govinda Temple: Located within the palace courtyard, this temple is famous for its terracotta carvings. The walls are covered in detailed scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata—think of it as a 19th-century comic book carved in clay. * Dol Mandir: A towering, four-story white structure that dominates the entrance to the complex. 📋 Quick Travel Tips | Location | Puthia Upazila, Rajshahi (on the Natore highway). | | Getting There | 40–50 minutes from Rajshahi city via bus or private car. | | Best Time | November to February (cooler weather) or May–July (mango season!). | | Duration | 1 hour is enough to see the main buildings. | | Photography | Excellent for architecture and portraits; no special permits usually needed for exteriors. | ⚖️ The Verdict Pros: * The highest concentration of historic temples in one walkable area in Bangladesh. * Incredible terracotta artistry that rivals the famous Kantajew Temple. * Less crowded and more "authentic" than many global heritage sites. Cons: * Maintenance is inconsistent; some areas feel neglected. * Limited tourist facilities (restaurants/restrooms) directly at the site. > Pro Tip: If you find a temple door locked, don't walk away! review_text_clean: In the mid seventeenth century one Kamadev Maitra served as tehsildar to the Puthia Raj family. Kamadev’s second son Raghunandan was selected by the Raja to be his agent at the court of Nawab Murshid Quli Khan, the overlord of all Bengal.[5] When the Nawab moved his court from Dhaka to what became known as Murshidabad he took Raghunandan with him and appointed him his Dewan or minister. The Nawab proceeded to confiscate the estates of zamindars who failed to conform to his new regulations, and a number of such estates were acquired by Ramjivan, the elder brother of his Dewan Raghunandan.[6] In due course Ramjivan was given the title of Raja and set up his headquarters in Natore. His estate was generally referred to as the "Rajshahi Zamindari". [5] The estate had an area of nearly 13,000 square miles and included not only much of North Bengal but also large parts of the areas later comprising the administrative districts of Murshidabad, Nadia, Jessore, Birbhum and Burdwan.[7] The first palace or Rajbari at Natore was built by Raja Ramjivan. The palace was surrounded by two sets of moats which are still extant.[5]After the division of the estate a separate palace was built for the junior branch of the dynasty. Many of the original buildings were destroyed by the earthquake of 1897 and subsequently rebuilt or replaced.[7] Ramjivan's Dewan Doyaram was granted landed estates and the title of Ray Raiyan by Nawab Murshid Quli Khan in recognition of his service in apprehending a recalcitrant zamindar named Sitaram Roy.[5][6] In due course Doyaram established his own dynasty the Dighapatia Raj with its own palace Dighapatia Palace[6]. Raja Ramjivan was succeeded by his adopted son Ramkanta.[5] After Raja Ramkanta's early death the Natore estate was ably managed by his widow, known as Rani Bhabani, who became famous for her good works.[5] In 1797, following the death of Rani Bhabani's adopted son Raja Ramkrishna, the Natore estate was divided between his two sons Bishwanath and Sibnath[5], and thenceforth both a Senior and a Junior royal house remained in existence until the abolition of all zamindar estates in 1950.[6]

review_text_clean: One of the oldest Rajbaris in Bangladesh (early 1700s), the magnificent but dilapidated Natore Rajbari was once the nerve-centre of undivided Bengal's second-biggest zamindari, which lost its sheen in the 19th century. The entire complex – moated by ponds and lined by centuries-old shady trees is actually a series of seven Rajbaris, four of which remain largely intact. One palace houses a police camp, another is a government office, while several others simply lie in ruins. The main palace block within the compound, called Boro Taraf ('big palace'; home of the elder patriarch of the family), is approached via a long avenue lined with impressively tall bottle palms, the white trunks of which resemble temple columns. To the rear of Boro Taraf are the crumbling walls of Rani Bhavani's Palace, which was the residence of the eponymous Rani Bhavani, the widowed wife of one of the Natore rajas who took up the reins of the estate and went on to become a very powerful administrator herself. To the far end of the complex stands a second palace block called Chhoto Taraf ('small palace'; for the younger brother of the family), consisting of two Rajbaris. The principal one faces a pond and is one of the most beautifully proportioned buildings in Bangladesh, although its cavernous central hall is now in a complete shambles. Entry is restricted, but peering through the broken window slats is allowed. The peaceful and idyllic gardens around the palaces are as much an attraction as the buildings themselves; bring a picnic to eat in the shade of a gnarled old tree. There are several large ponds here that form an interesting centrepiece, around which are a couple of Hindu temples, one dedicated to Kali and another to Shiva.

review_text_clean: প্রাকৃতিক এবং কৃত্রিমতার মেলবন্ধনে গঠিত একটা পার্ক।দিন দিন তাদের প্রবেশ ফি বেড়েই চলছে।প্রথমে ২০টাকা ছিল এখন ৪০টাকা,স্টাফদের আচরণ তেমন প্রফেশনাল না।টিকেট কেটে যাবার পরও,ভিতরে ওয়াশরুমে যেতে হয় আবার টিকেট কেটে।ভিতরের পরিবেশ সুন্দর,বিশাল জায়গা নিয়ে গঠিত।প্রধান আকর্ষণ ঝুলন্ত ব্রিজ,এছাড়া লেক,বাচ্চাদের বিনোদনের ব্যবস্থা,খাবারের দোকান রয়েছে।ওভারওল মোটামুটি।

review_text_clean: পাহাড়ী সৌন্দর্যের শহর খাগড়াছড়ি জেলার জিরো পয়েন্ট থেকে ৩ কি.মি দূরে খাগড়াছড়ি পার্বত্য জেলা পরিষদের তত্ত্বাবধানে নির্মিত সবুজ বেষ্টনীতে ঘেরা মনোরম সুন্দর পরিবেশে হর্টিকালচার হ্যারিটেজ পার্ক শহরের অন্যতম বিনোদন কেন্দ্র হিসেবে সুপরিচিত। কিভাবে যাওয়া যায় খাগড়াছড়ি শহর থেকে রিকসায় বা ইজি বাইকে সহজেই যাওয়া যায়। বিস্তারিত জেলা শহরের জিরোমাইল এলাকায় ২২ একর পাহাড় জুড়ে নির্মাণ করা হয়েছে এই হর্টিকালচার হ্যারিটেজ পার্ক। এই পার্কে রয়েছে অসাধারণ সুন্দর একটি ঝুলন্ত ব্রিজ এবং বড় একটি লেক। হর্টিকালচার পার্ক এর ভিতরের পরিবেশ বেশ মনোরম। পার্কের পশ্চিম পাশ থেকে খাগড়াছড়ি শহরের ভিউটা অসাধারণ। এছাড়াও পার্কের ভিতরে রয়েছে দোলনা, ওয়াচ টাওয়ার, ফুলের বাগান ও বিভিন্ন প্রজাতির ফল গাছ।

review_text_clean: খাগড়াছড়ি পার্বত্য জেলা পরিষদ হটিকালচার পার্কে।💁‍♂️ পার্কে টিকিট (৪০ টাকা) নিয়ে ভিতরে প্রবেশ করে প্রথমেই ঝুলন্ত ব্রিজের উপরে হেঁটে ওপাশে গিয়ে একটি দোলনায় দোল খেলাম। ঠিক যেন ছোট্ট পিচ্ছি হয়ে গেছি আমি। এই হটিকালচার পার্কে প্রায় সব ধরনের গাছের সাথে পরিচয় হবে। শরতের ফুলগুলো আভা ছড়িয়েছে পুরো হৃদয় জুড়ে। হেঁটে হেঁটে এগুচ্ছি আর নয়নাভিরাম প্রকৃতির সৌন্দর্য উপভোগ করছি ঠিক এভাবে 🎷 🌼কুঞ্জবনে অপর সবাই ফূর্তি করে পুলক প্রাণ শারাব হাতে শুনছে বসে "কুহু-কুহু" কোয়েল তান, সেই সে খুশির জলসা থেকে নির্জনে সে অনেক দূর তোমার প্রেমের দিওয়ানারাও শুনতে চাহে "হু হু" র সুর! তোমার প্রেমের পতংদের দাও দহনের সাধ আবার বিজলী দিয়ে জাগাও তাদের সুপ্ত নীরব হৃদয় তার।🍃 কিছুদূর পর "I❤️Khagrachhari" লেখাটি দেখে পুলকিত হলাম (ব্লগে নয়নাভিরাম ভিডিও দেখতে পারবেন)। এখানকার প্রশাসন কত যত্ন ও পরিকল্পনা করে এই পার্কটি সাজিয়েছে। বাংলাদেশের সব জেলার প্রশাসন যদি এমন পরিকল্পিত ও যত্নবান হতো তাহলে আমার বাংলাদেশের প্রতিটি জেলা হয়ে উঠতো একেকটি পর্যটন উপলক্ষ। ধন্যবাদ জনাচ্ছি খাগড়াছড়ি প্রশাসন কে, যারা এত সুন্দর করে পার্কটি সাজিয়েছেন। এখানে প্রায় ২ ঘন্টা থকার পর আসার সময় আখের শরবত খেয়ে আবারো প্রাণ জুড়িয়ে নিলাম। সময় এখন দুপুর ২ টা।🙄 🗑আমি ভ্রমণের সময় আমার ব্যাগে সবসময় পলি রাখি, কারণ আমার ব্যাবহৃত বিস্কুট, কেক বা অন্য কোন কিছুর প্যাকেট অথবা ময়লা এই পলিতে রাখি এবং যখনি ডাস্টবিন দেখবো ওখানে এগুলো ফেলে দিবো। এভাবেই পরিষ্কার থাকুক আমাদের বাংলাদেশ ।🇧🇩

review_text_clean: 1. স্থান পাহাড়ী সৌন্দর্যের শহর খাগড়াছড়ি জেলার জিরো পয়েন্ট থেকে ৩ কি.মি দূরে খাগড়াছড়ি পার্বত্য জেলা পরিষদের তত্ত্বাবধানে নির্মিত সবুজ বেষ্টনীতে ঘেরা মনোরম সুন্দর পরিবেশে হর্টিকালচার হ্যারিটেজ পার্ক শহরের অন্যতম বিনোদন কেন্দ্র হিসেবে সুপরিচিত। 2. কিভাবে যাওয়া যায় খাগড়াছড়ি শহর থেকে রিকসায় বা ইজি বাইকে সহজেই যাওয়া যায়। 3. বিস্তারিত জেলা শহরের জিরোমাইল এলাকায় ২২ একর পাহাড় জুড়ে নির্মাণ করা হয়েছে এই হর্টিকালচার হ্যারিটেজ পার্ক। এই পার্কে রয়েছে অসাধারণ সুন্দর একটি ঝুলন্ত ব্রিজ এবং বড় একটি লেক। হর্টিকালচার পার্ক এর ভিতরের পরিবেশ বেশ মনোরম। পার্কের পশ্চিম পাশ থেকে খাগড়াছড়ি শহরের ভিউটা অসাধারণ। এছাড়াও পার্কের ভিতরে রয়েছে দোলনা, ওয়াচ টাওয়ার, ফুলের বাগান ও বিভিন্ন প্রজাতির ফল গাছ।
