Kuakata is a picturesque coastal town located in the Kalapara Upazila of Patuakhali District, in southern Bangladesh. Famously known as the “Daughter of the Sea” (Sagor Kannya), Kuakata is one of the few places in the world where visitors can enjoy both the sunrise and sunset over the sea from the same beach. The Kuakata Sea Beach stretches approximately 18 kilometers in length and 3 kilometers in width, offering wide sandy shores lined with coconut trees and a peaceful atmosphere. It attracts both local and international tourists who come to experience its natural beauty, tranquility, and unique seascape. Apart from the beach, Kuakata is home to natural forests, such as the Gangamati Reserved Forest and Jhau Tree Plantation, which are popular for hiking and wildlife viewing. The nearby Kuakata Ecopark and Kuakata National Park are also important ecological attractions. Kuakata has a rich cultural heritage, particularly tied to the Rakhine Buddhist community, who settled here centuries ago. Tourists can visit ancient Buddhist temples, traditional Rakhine villages, and sacred sites like the century-old Buddha statue and natural wells believed to have historical significance. The best time to visit Kuakata is during the cooler months from November to March, when the weather is pleasant and the beach is most enjoyable. Traditional festivals like Rash Purnima and Maghi Purnima bring added cultural color, often featuring fairs and religious ceremonies. Kuakata is accessible by road and river. Buses and launches operate regularly from Dhaka and other major cities. Efforts are ongoing to improve tourism facilities and preserve the natural environment, making Kuakata an increasingly popular destination for nature lovers and peace seekers.

The Paharpur Buddhist Vihara, also known as Somapura Mahavihara, is one of the most significant archaeological sites in South Asia. Located in the Naogaon district and it stands as a testament to the rise of Mahayana Buddhism in Bengal and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. Built by Dharmapala, the second king of the Pala dynasty (c. 770–810 AD). It served as a premier intellectual center, attracting scholars and monks from across the Buddhist world, including China and Tibet, until the 12th century. The complex is massive, covering nearly 27 acres (11 hectares). Its layout is characterized by a Central Shrine a lofty, cross-shaped structure that rises in three receding terraces to a height of about 72 feet. It is decorated with terracotta plaques depicting daily life, mythology, and deities and a vast square courtyard measuring approximately 900 feet on each side. The outer walls are composed of 177 individual cells where monks lived and meditated. It is famous for its intricate stone sculptures and terracotta art, which provide a rare window into the social and religious life of ancient Bengal.

Kaptai Water and Electricity Center, the only hydroelectric power plant in Bangladesh is situated in Kaptai, which is 50km from the port city Chittagong. Kaptai Upazila is bounded by rangamati sadar and kawkhali upazilas on the north, Rajasthali Upazila on the south, belaichhari on the east, rangunia and Kawkhali Upazila on the west. The main water bodies of Kaptai Sub District are Karnafuli River and the Kaptai Lake. It is a brilliant spot for tourists; they will be able to witness the majestic Water and Electricity Center as well as the beautiful Kaptai Lake. There are trees all round the surrounding area of the Kaptai Hydro electric power plant; tourists can take a walk into the natural retreat that is stated in Kaptai and take pictures. The Kaptai Water and Electricity Center has an arc-shaped canal which holds the river Rinkhyong at the upstream and the fountain Freengkhyang at the downstream. It is built in 1962, financed by the USA and built by a joint effort of International Engineering Company (IEC) and Utah International Inc. The design includes an earth-filled dam which is 45.7m high, 670.6m long and 7.6m wide, that holds water from the upstream which is released by 16 gate spillways (each 12.2m by 11.3 m) and tunnels through a spiral route that activates and rotates the turbines to generate electricity. The current capacity of this plant is 230MW, which powers Chittagong and adds to the national grid, which saves foreign currency for importing manufactured goods and expands national industries. It also helps to power water pumps for irrigation and helps cultivate various breeds of fish. The dam helps prevent flooding during Monsoon season between June and October, thus saving numerous lives. Most of the power is generated during this Monsoon season when the dam holds most water. Nonetheless, typhoons and seasonal storms cause shifts in tidal waves that caused overflow in the dam area causing damage to crops and properties, which the government compensates on humanitarian grounds. Tourists can take an exciting boat ride in the Kaptai Lake and explore and witness the wonderful natural sceneries of the area surrounding the Lake. From the Kaptai Boat Terminal tourist can make a sweet journey of the Kaptai Lake. There are also excellent restaurants near the lake where tourists can have their Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner. Guliakhali Sea Beach, located in Sitakunda, is undeniably one of the most unique and photogenic natural spots in Bangladesh because it defies the traditional definition of a beach by swapping golden sand for a stunning carpet of lush green grass that stretches right up to the water's edge. Unlike the crashing waves of Cox's Bazar, the environment here feels more like a serene mangrove swamp, characterized by scattered Keora trees and meandering winding canals that fill up with water during high tide, creating a surreal landscape that looks almost like a painting. This "Muradpur Beach," as it is locally known, is a paradise for photographers and nature enthusiasts who want to witness the dramatic contrast between the vibrant green ground, the dark muddy banks, and the vast open sea, especially during sunset when the light hits the water perfectly. However, visitors must come prepared for a bit of an adventure because the terrain is naturally muddy and slippery; you will likely need to navigate across small, muddy creeks or hire a local boat to cross the larger channels if the tide is high, so wearing expensive sneakers or formal clothes is a terrible idea—stick to rubber sandals or go barefoot. It is also important to note that this is not a swimming beach in the traditional sense, as the water is murky and the floor is muddy rather than sandy, making it better suited for walking, relaxing, and enjoying the breeze rather than taking a dip. The road leading to the beach from the Sitakunda market is narrow and can get congested, and amenities like decent washrooms or high-quality restaurants are virtually non-existent near the shore, so carrying your own water and snacks is essential. Despite the lack of commercial facilities and the muddy feet you will inevitably go home with, the raw, untouched beauty of Guliakhali offers a refreshing and distinctively calm atmosphere that makes the journey absolutely worth it for anyone exploring the Chittagong region.

Karamjal Eco-Tourism Center is an awesome part of Sundarbans. Karamjal, an attractive tourist destination of the forest department, is located in the Sundarbans on a 30 hectare land on the banks of the Pashur River, a short distance from the Mongla seaport. Karamjal has been developed by the Forest Department as a model for the Sundarbans. Hundreds of tourists come here every day. Karamjal is the perfect place to visit the Sundarbans in one day and get an idea of ​​the Sundarbans. The main attractions here are deer, crocodiles, monkeys, wooden trails, towers, boating, fishermen’s fishing scenes. The only natural crocodile breeding center in the country is located here. The tourist center is located at a distance of about 80 km from Khulna and about 8 km from Mongla by the river. In addition to an eco-tourism center, there are deer and crocodile breeding and rearing centers. If you take an engine boat from Mongla, you can reach Karamjal jetty in one to one and a half hours. The huge map at the beginning of the tourist center will give a good idea about the Sundarbans.

​Karamjal is the most accessible and popular eco-tourism center within the Sundarbans East Wildlife Sanctuary. Located on the banks of the Pashur River, just a short boat ride from Mongla, it serves as an essential introduction to the world's largest mangrove forest. It is often the first stop for travelers looking to experience the unique biodiversity of this UNESCO World Heritage site without venturing deep into the core forest zones. ​The highlight of Karamjal is its extensive wooden trail (canopy walk) that snakes through the dense mangrove thicket. This elevated walkway allows visitors to observe the complex root systems of Sundari and Kewra trees and catch glimpses of the forest's inhabitants—such as rhesus macaques, colorful kingfishers, and spotted deer—from a safe and eco-friendly distance. The air here is thick with the scent of salt and earth, providing a sensory immersion into the "Green Wall" of Bangladesh. ​Karamjal also houses the country's only Saltwater Crocodile Breeding Center and a Turtle Breeding Center. These facilities play a crucial role in the conservation of the endangered "Batagur Baska" turtles and the region's apex reptilian predators. A climb up the forest's observation tower offers a breathtaking panoramic view of the winding Pashur River and the endless canopy of green. For those visiting the Khulna region, Karamjal offers a vital balance of education, conservation, and the raw, natural beauty of the mangroves.
